eastphalia.s: Eastphalia (Ostfalen) was the eastern division of Old Saxony, between the Weser–Leine region and the Elbe and Saale, around modern Brunswick, Hildesheim and Magdeburg. With Westphalia and Angria it made up the land of the Saxons conquered by Charlemagne.

ewe-people.s: The Ewe are a West African people of south-eastern Ghana, southern Togo and parts of Benin, speaking the Ewe language of the Gbe group. Their traditions trace a migration from Notsie in Togo, after which they formed many small states, such as Anlo.

east-slavs.s: The East Slavs are the Slavic peoples of eastern Europe from whom the Russians, Ukrainians and Belarusians descend. In the early Middle Ages they formed tribes such as the Polianians, Drevlianians and Krivichians, described in the Primary Chronicle, and in the 9th and 10th…

ellalan.s: Ellalan, called Elara in the Pali chronicles, was a Tamil prince from the Chola country who ruled Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka for about 44 years in the 2nd century BCE. The Mahavamsa remembers him as a just ruler, although he was not a Buddhist.

eunones.s: Eunones was king of the Aorsi, a Sarmatian people north of the Caucasus, in the mid-1st century CE. In the Bosporan war of 49 CE he sided with Rome against the deposed Bosporan king Mithridates and his Siracan allies under Zorsines.

eadgyth.s: Eadgyth, also known as Edith of England, was a daughter of King Edward the Elder of the English and the first wife of Otto I, king of East Francia. Married around 930, she was respected for her piety and generosity, and she died in 946.

echizen-province.s: Echizen was an old province of Japan on the Sea of Japan coast, now the northern part of Fukui Prefecture. In the Sengoku period it was ruled by the Asakura clan from Ichijōdani until Oda Nobunaga destroyed them in 1573.

eurymedon-river.s: The Eurymedon, now the Köprüçay, is a river of southern Turkey that flows from the Taurus mountains to the Mediterranean through ancient Pamphylia. The city of Aspendos stood near its lower course, and Selge lay above its gorge.

euripides.s: Euripides was an Athenian tragic playwright, active from 455 BCE until his death in about 406 BCE. Eighteen or nineteen of his plays survive, more than of any other Greek tragedian, including Medea, Hippolytus, The Trojan Women and The Bacchae.

english-channel.s: The English Channel is the arm of the Atlantic Ocean that separates southern England from northern France, joining the North Sea at the Strait of Dover, about 33 km wide. It has long been a route for trade and migration and a barrier against invasion, crossed by Caesar, by the…

eppillus.d: late 1st century BCE – early 1st century CE
eppillus.s: Eppillus was a British king of the late 1st century BCE and early 1st century CE known from his coins, which call him a son of Commius. He appears to have ruled at Calleva Atrebatum and later in Kent.

eure.s: The Eure is a river of northern France, about 228 km long, which rises in the Perche hills and flows north past Chartres to join the Seine above Rouen. It gives its name to the departments of Eure, whose capital is Évreux, and Eure-et-Loir.

evreux.s: Évreux is a city in Normandy, northern France, and the capital of the Eure department. It began as Mediolanum Aulercorum, the Roman capital of the Gallic Eburovices, from whom its name derives.

eauze.s: Eauze is a small town in the Gers department of Gascony, south-western France. As Elusa it was the chief town of the Aquitanian Elusates and in late antiquity the capital of the Roman province of Novempopulana and seat of its metropolitan bishop.

estonian-provincial-assembly.s: The Estonian Provincial Assembly, or Maapäev, was the elected council of the Autonomous Governorate of Estonia, created after the February Revolution in Russia and first meeting in July 1917. On 28 November 1917 it declared itself the supreme authority in Estonia before…

estonian-salvation-committee.s: The Estonian Salvation Committee was a three-member executive body formed in February 1918 by the Council of Elders of the Estonian Provincial Assembly, made up of Konstantin Päts, Jüri Vilms and Konstantin Konik. On 24 February 1918, between the Bolshevik withdrawal and the…

ephesus.s: Ephesus was an ancient Greek city on the west coast of Anatolia, near modern Selçuk in Turkey, famed for its Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders of the World. Under Rome it was the capital of the province of Asia and an early centre of Christianity.

el-rizk-mosque.s: The El Rizk Mosque is a mosque in Hasankeyf, in south-eastern Turkey, built in 1409 under the Ayyubid ruler al-Adil Sulayman. Its tall minaret, decorated with carved inscriptions and muqarnas, became one of the town's landmarks on the bank of the Tigris.

erzurum.s: Erzurum is a city on a high plateau in eastern Turkey, near the sources of the Euphrates. Known in late antiquity as Theodosiopolis, it guarded the routes between Anatolia, Iran and the Caucasus and was ruled in turn by Byzantines, Arabs, Armenians, the Saltukids and the Seljuks.

eugen-zintgraff.s: Eugen Zintgraff was a German explorer and colonial agent in Kamerun. In 1889 he reached the Bamenda grassfields and formed an alliance with Fon Galega I of Bali-Nyonga, aiming to recruit labour and open trade routes for German colonial interests.

elliott-cresson.s: Elliott Cresson was a Quaker merchant and philanthropist from Philadelphia and a leading advocate of the American Colonization Society, which settled free African Americans in West Africa. He toured Britain in the early 1830s to raise funds for the cause.

erich-muhsam.s: Erich Mühsam was a German anarchist writer, poet and satirist. He helped proclaim the Bavarian Soviet Republic in April 1919 and was sentenced to fifteen years' imprisonment, serving until an amnesty in 1924.

eulmash-shakin-shumi.s: Eulmash-shakin-shumi was king of Babylon from about 1004 to 988 BCE and founder of the short-lived Bazi Dynasty, which followed the Second Sealand Dynasty. He reigned for about seventeen years, the longest of the dynasty.

erbil.s: Erbil, ancient Arbela, is the capital of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq. Its citadel mound has been inhabited for thousands of years and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

etsu-nupe.s: Etsu Nupe is the title of the traditional ruler of the Nupe people of central Nigeria. Since the Fulani conquest of Nupe in the 19th century, the title has been held by emirs of the dynasty of Mallam Dendo, ruling from Bida.

erhard-von-queis.s: Erhard von Queis was bishop of Pomesania in Prussia from 1523 until his death in 1529. A lawyer from Silesia, he adopted Lutheranism and introduced reforms in his diocese.

emilia.s: Emilia is a historic region of northern Italy between the Po and the Apennines, named after the Roman road, the Via Aemilia, that crosses it. Its cities include Parma, Piacenza, Modena and Reggio.

emilio-garrastazu-medici.s: Emílio Garrastazu Médici was a Brazilian general who served as president from 1969 to 1974, the harshest period of the military dictatorship. His government used censorship, torture and killings to destroy the armed left, while the 'Brazilian miracle' brought very rapid…

eoka.s: EOKA, the National Organisation of Cypriot Fighters, was a Greek Cypriot guerrilla organisation that fought British rule in Cyprus from 1955 to 1959 with the aim of enosis, union with Greece. Led by George Grivas and backed by Archbishop Makarios III, it waged a campaign of…

enver-pasha.s: Enver Pasha was an Ottoman officer and politician, a leader of the Young Turk Revolution of 1908 and of the Committee of Union and Progress. As war minister from 1914 he took the Ottoman Empire into the First World War on Germany's side and led the disastrous Sarikamish campaign.

eid-al-ghadir.s: Eid al-Ghadir is a Shia Muslim festival held on 18 Dhu al-Hijja to commemorate the Prophet Muhammad's sermon at Ghadir Khumm in 632, in which Shia Muslims see the designation of Ali ibn Abi Talib as his successor. The Buyid ruler Mu'izz al-Dawla made it a public celebration in…

eifel.s: The Eifel is a low mountain range in western Germany, between Aachen, Trier and Koblenz, extending into eastern Belgium. Its volcanic landscape includes crater lakes known as maars.

estero-bay.s: Estero Bay is a shallow estuary on the south-west coast of Florida, between Fort Myers Beach and Bonita Springs, sheltered by barrier islands. Its mangrove waters supported the Calusa, whose capital stood on Mound Key in the bay.

einsiedeln-abbey.s: Einsiedeln Abbey is a Benedictine monastery in the canton of Schwyz, founded in 934 on the site where the hermit Saint Meinrad had lived. Its shrine of the Black Madonna made it one of the chief pilgrimage centres of Europe.

eastern-cape.s: The Eastern Cape is a province of South Africa, created in 1994 from the eastern part of the Cape Province and the former homelands of Transkei and Ciskei. Its capital is Bhisho and its largest cities are Gqeberha and East London.

estella-lizarra.s: Estella-Lizarra is a town in Navarre, northern Spain, on the Ega river and the pilgrim route to Santiago de Compostela, founded by King Sancho Ramírez in 1090. Rich in Romanesque churches, it was a stronghold of Carlism.

euripus-strait.s: The Euripus is the narrow strait between the island of Euboea and mainland Greece, only about 40 metres wide at Chalcis. It is famous for its strong tidal currents, which reverse direction several times a day and puzzled ancient writers.

eder-river.s: The Eder is a river of Germany, about 177 km long, rising in the Rothaar mountains of North Rhine-Westphalia and flowing east through Hesse past Waldeck to join the Fulda near Kassel. Its upper hills were Chattian land in Roman times, and the castle of Waldeck above it gave…

eiso.s: Eiso is a semi-legendary king of Okinawa, said in Ryukyuan chronicles to have reigned at Urasoe from 1260 to 1299 as founder of the Eiso dynasty. The chronicles describe him as a wise ruler who received tribute from outlying islands, surveyed the land and built a Buddhist…

earl-of-clanricarde.s: Earl of Clanricarde is a title in the Peerage of Ireland created in 1543 for Ulick na gCeann Burke, chief of the Burkes of south County Galway, under Henry VIII's policy of surrender and regrant. The earls held lands around Loughrea and Portumna, and the later holders were…

etruria.s: Etruria was the region of central Italy inhabited by the Etruscans, bounded by the Arno, the Tiber and the Tyrrhenian Sea and covering most of modern Tuscany with parts of Lazio and Umbria. Its independent city-states, among them Veii, Tarquinii, Vulci, Caere and Clusium,…

eleuthera.s: Eleuthera is a long, narrow island in the Bahamas, east of New Providence. In 1648 Puritan settlers from Bermuda under William Sayle, the Eleutheran Adventurers, founded the first English settlement in the Bahamas there, naming it after the Greek word for freedom.

eureka-rebellion.s: The Eureka Rebellion was a revolt by gold miners at Ballarat in Victoria in 1854 against the costly miners' licences and the conduct of the authorities. Led by Peter Lalor, the miners built a stockade and raised the Southern Cross flag, but soldiers and police stormed it on 3…

ecueracapa.s: Ecueracapa was a Comanche chief who emerged as the leading spokesman of the western Comanche in the 1780s. In 1786 he negotiated a peace with Juan Bautista de Anza, governor of Spanish New Mexico, which ended decades of raiding there and allied the Comanche with Spain against…

enguerrand-vii-de-coucy.s: Enguerrand VII de Coucy was a French nobleman and soldier, lord of one of the great baronies of northern France and son-in-law of Edward III of England. He led mercenary companies in Switzerland and Italy, where in 1384 he took Arezzo and sold it to Florence.

elche.s: Elche is a city in the province of Alicante, south-eastern Spain, near the site of Iberian and Roman Ilici at La Alcudia, where the Lady of Elche was found. Its Palm Grove, planted in the Islamic period, and its medieval mystery play, the Misteri d'Elx, are both recognised by…

exxonmobil.s: ExxonMobil is an American oil and gas company formed in 1999 by the merger of Exxon and Mobil, both descended from John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil.

erispoe.s: Erispoe was ruler of Brittany from 851 to 857, son of Nominoe. Soon after succeeding his father he defeated Charles the Bald at the Battle of Jengland in 851, and the Treaty of Angers that followed recognised him as king, with Rennes, Nantes and the Pays de Retz.

eleusis.s: Eleusis is an ancient town in Attica, about 18 kilometres north-west of Athens, now called Elefsina. It was home to the sanctuary of Demeter and Persephone where the Eleusinian Mysteries, the most famous secret religious rites of the Greek world, were celebrated for many…

eustace-ii-count-of-boulogne.s: Eustace II was count of Boulogne from about 1049 and one of the leading allies of William the Conqueror at the Battle of Hastings in 1066, where he appears on the Bayeux Tapestry. He received large estates in England.

emden.s: Emden is a port city in East Frisia, Lower Saxony, Germany, near the mouth of the Ems on the Dollart bay. In the 16th century it received many Protestant refugees from the Netherlands and became a centre of the Reformed Church, sometimes called the 'Geneva of the North'.

eitel-friedrich-ii-count-of-hohenzollern.n: Eitel Friedrich II, Count of Hohenzollern
eitel-friedrich-ii-count-of-hohenzollern.s: Eitel Friedrich II (1452–1512) was Count of Hohenzollern and a close adviser and commander of Emperor Maximilian I, who made him the first judge of the Imperial Chamber Court in 1495 and hereditary chamberlain of the Empire. He restored the Swabian Hohenzollerns' fortunes…

ernest-ii-duke-of-swabia.s: Ernest II (c. 1010–1030) was Duke of Swabia from 1015 and a stepson of Emperor Conrad II.

elisabeth-of-gorlitz.s: Elisabeth of Görlitz (1390–1451) was Duchess of Luxembourg, a niece of Emperor Sigismund of the House of Luxembourg. She held the duchy in pledge from 1411 and married first Anthony of Burgundy, Duke of Brabant, and then John III of Bavaria-Straubing.

elias-i-count-of-maine.s: Elias of La Flèche (died 1110) was Count of Maine from the 1090s. He resisted William Rufus of England, who captured him in 1098, and after his release recovered Maine in 1100.

eisleben.s: Eisleben, officially Lutherstadt Eisleben, is a town in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany, east of the Harz. Martin Luther was born there in 1483 and died there in 1546, and the houses of his birth and death are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

eberhard-ii-count-of-the-mark.n: Eberhard II, Count of the Mark
eberhard-ii-count-of-the-mark.s: Eberhard II (c. 1255–1308) was Count of the Mark from 1277.

eberhard-iv-count-of-wurttemberg.s: Eberhard IV (1388–1419), called the Younger, was Count of Württemberg from 1417. In 1397, as a child, he was betrothed to Henriette of Montbéliard, heiress of the County of Montbéliard, and their marriage brought Montbéliard to the House of Württemberg, which held it until 1793.

elmshorn.s: Elmshorn is a town in the Pinneberg district of Schleswig-Holstein, on the Krückau about 30 km north-west of Hamburg. In the 17th and 18th centuries it belonged to the County of Rantzau and grew as a market, shipping and craft town, later becoming an industrial centre.

east-tyrol.s: East Tyrol is a district of the Austrian state of Tyrol, centred on Lienz. It belonged to the counts of Gorizia until 1500, when it passed to the Habsburgs and was joined to Tyrol, and it has been cut off from North Tyrol since 1919, when South Tyrol went to Italy.

eleanor-of-castile.s: Eleanor of Castile was Queen of England as the first wife of Edward I, whom she married in 1254. A daughter of Ferdinand III of Castile, she inherited the county of Ponthieu from her mother in 1279.

eleanor-of-arborea.s: Eleanor of Arborea was a Sardinian ruler who governed the Judicate of Arborea for her young sons from 1383 until her death in 1404. Daughter of Mariano IV, she continued the war against the Crown of Aragon and in 1392 issued the Carta de Logu, a law code in Sardinian that…

ephorus.s: Ephorus of Cyme was a Greek historian of the 4th century BCE, said to have been a pupil of Isocrates. His Histories in 30 books were the first universal history, arranged by subject from the return of the Heracleidae to 340 BCE.

emperor-qinzong.s: Emperor Qinzong was the ninth emperor of the Song dynasty of China, reigning from 1126 to 1127 after his father Huizong abdicated during the Jurchen invasion. When Jin armies captured Kaifeng in the Jingkang incident of 1127, he and Huizong were carried off to the north with…

eohric.s: Eohric was a Danish king of East Anglia, ruling the Viking kingdom established by Guthrum. He joined Æthelwold, a rebel cousin of Edward the Elder, in raiding Mercia and Wessex, and was killed in the Battle of the Holme around 902, although the Danes held the field.

el-geneina.s: El Geneina is a city in western Sudan, the capital of West Darfur state, close to the border with Chad. It became the capital of the Masalit sultanate under Sultan Muhammad Bahr al-Din, known as Andoka, in the early 20th century, and the sultan's family kept a role there under…

expulsion-of-the-deisi.s: The Expulsion of the Déisi is an Old Irish tale, surviving in versions from the 8th century onwards, about the origins of the Déisi. It tells how they were driven from their lands in Brega near Tara after a quarrel with the high king Cormac mac Airt and wandered south, some…

east-java.s: East Java is a province of Indonesia occupying the eastern part of the island of Java and the island of Madura, with its capital at Surabaya. It was the heartland of the Hindu-Buddhist kingdoms of Kediri, Singhasari and Majapahit, whose capital lay at Trowulan.

esau-de-buondelmonti.s: Esau de' Buondelmonti was a Florentine nobleman who ruled Ioannina in Epirus from 1385 to 1411. He married Maria Angelina Doukaina Palaiologina, widow of the murdered ruler Thomas Preljubović, and governed with Byzantine support.

enki.s: Enki was the Sumerian god of fresh water, crafts, wisdom and magic, known to the Akkadians as Ea. His chief temple, the E-abzu, stood at Eridu in southern Mesopotamia, which was regarded as his city.

etichonids.s: The Etichonids were a Frankish noble family descended from Adalrich, also called Eticho, Duke of Alsace in the later 7th century. They held the Alsatian duchy until about 740 and founded or endowed monasteries such as Hohenburg, Honau and Murbach.

engelbert-ii-of-berg.s: Engelbert II of Berg was Count of Berg and, from 1216, Archbishop of Cologne. Emperor Frederick II made him regent of Germany and guardian of his son Henry (VII) in 1220.

engelbert-i-of-nassau.s: Engelbert I was Count of Nassau-Dillenburg and Lord of Breda. In 1403 he married Johanna van Polanen, heiress of Breda, which gave the Nassau family large estates in the Low Countries and began the line that led to William the Silent and the House of Orange-Nassau.

edict-of-union.s: The Edict of Union, issued by King Francis I in August 1532 after a request from the Estates of Brittany meeting at Vannes, permanently joined the Duchy of Brittany to the Kingdom of France. It guaranteed Breton privileges, such as the consent of the Estates to taxation, which…

elizabeth-lucretia-duchess-of-teschen.s: Elizabeth Lucretia was Duchess of Cieszyn, or Teschen, from 1625 to 1653, the last ruler of the Cieszyn branch of the Piast dynasty. She succeeded her brother Frederick William and governed the duchy through the hardships of the Thirty Years' War.

emmerich-am-rhein.s: Emmerich am Rhein is a town on the lower Rhine in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, on the Dutch border. It received town rights in 1233, later belonged to the Duchy of Cleves and was a member of the Hanseatic League.

ercole-i-d-este.s: Ercole I d'Este was Duke of Ferrara, Modena and Reggio from 1471 to 1505. A patron of the poet Boiardo, of music and of theatre, he commissioned the Addizione Erculea, a planned extension of Ferrara.

eberhard-of-franconia.s: Eberhard was Duke of Franconia from 918, the brother of King Conrad I. He carried the royal insignia to Henry of Saxony, supporting his election as king in 919, but later rebelled against Henry's son Otto I.

eberhard-i-count-of-wurttemberg.s: Eberhard I, called the Illustrious, was Count of Württemberg from 1279 to 1325. He fought the kings of Germany and the Swabian imperial cities, and lost most of his lands in 1312 to forces acting for Emperor Henry VII, but recovered them after the emperor's death.

eberhard-of-friuli.s: Eberhard of Friuli was a Frankish nobleman of the Unruoching family who became Margrave of Friuli around 846. He married Gisela, daughter of Emperor Louis the Pious, defended the march against Slavs and Saracens, and corresponded with scholars such as Hrabanus Maurus.

elisabeth-farnese.s: Elisabeth Farnese (1692–1766) was queen of Spain as the second wife of Philip V from 1714, and heiress of the Farnese dukes of Parma. A dominant figure at the Spanish court, she used war and diplomacy to win Italian thrones for her sons, securing Naples and Sicily for Charles…

eric-ii-duke-of-pomerania.s: Eric II (c. 1425–1474) was a Duke of Pomerania of the Griffin dynasty who ruled Pomerania-Wolgast and, after the death of his relative King Eric of Pomerania in 1459, also the eastern lands around Stolp.

ernest-frederick-duke-of-saxe-coburg-saa.s: Ernest Frederick was Duke of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld from 1764 until his death in 1800. His small duchy was so heavily in debt that an imperial debt commission supervised its finances during much of his reign.

eisenberg-thuringia.s: Eisenberg is a small town in the Saale-Holzland district of Thuringia, Germany, between Gera and Jena. From 1680 to 1707 it was the residence of Duke Christian of Saxe-Eisenberg, who rebuilt Christiansburg Palace and gave it a richly decorated Baroque chapel.

elisabethenburg-palace.s: Elisabethenburg Palace is the former residence of the dukes of Saxe-Meiningen in Meiningen, Thuringia. Duke Bernhard I built it between 1682 and 1692 and named it after his second wife, Elisabeth Eleonore.

erfurt-division.s: The Erfurt Division was the partition of the Ernestine Saxon lands agreed at Erfurt in November 1572. the Weimar line of Duke John William and his son Frederick William I kept Weimar and the surrounding lands, while the sons of his deposed brother John Frederick II received…

erchanger-duke-of-swabia.s: Erchanger was a Swabian count who led opposition to King Conrad I of East Francia. In 915 he defeated the king's supporters at Wahlwies and was proclaimed Duke of Swabia.

euin-of-trent.s: Euin was the first Lombard Duke of Trent, named by Paul the Deacon, ruling from around 569 or 575 until his death in 595. He defended the Adige valley against Frankish invasions in the 570s and 580s and married a daughter of the Bavarian duke Garibald I, linking Trent with…

elbistan.s: Elbistan is a town in Kahramanmaraş Province, south-eastern Turkey, on a high plain of the eastern Taurus. In 1277 the Mamluk sultan Baybars defeated a Mongol and Seljuk army nearby at the Battle of Elbistan.

exeter.s: Exeter is a cathedral city on the River Exe and the county town of Devon in south-west England. It began around 55 CE as a fortress of the Roman legio II Augusta, and when the army moved on it became Isca Dumnoniorum, the civitas capital of the Dumnonii.

exeter-new-hampshire.s: Exeter is a town in Rockingham County, New Hampshire, in the United States. It was founded in 1638 by the dissenting minister John Wheelwright and his followers after their banishment from the Massachusetts Bay Colony.

ethical-policy.s: The Ethical Policy was the colonial policy of the Netherlands in the Dutch East Indies announced by Queen Wilhelmina in 1901. Following criticism that the Netherlands owed a debt to the colony, it promised irrigation, education and emigration from crowded Java.

edward-bruce.s: Edward Bruce was a younger brother of Robert the Bruce, King of Scots. In 1315 he invaded Ireland with a Scottish army, seeking to open a second front against England, and was proclaimed High King of Ireland by his Irish allies in 1316.

edict-of-torda.s: The Edict of Torda was a decree of the diet of the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom, meeting at Torda (Turda) in Transylvania in January 1568 under John Sigismund Zápolya. It allowed each community to choose preachers according to its own beliefs and forbade persecution on grounds of…

emperor-yuan-of-jin.s: Emperor Yuan of Jin, born Sima Rui, was the founding emperor of the Eastern Jin dynasty. A member of the Jin imperial clan and Prince of Langye, he was posted to Jianye in 307 and, backed by the Wang clan led by Wang Dao, became the rallying point of the south as northern…

eblana.s: Eblana is a place named on the east coast of Ireland in the Geography of Ptolemy, compiled around 150 CE, as a town of the Eblani people. Older writers took it to be Dublin, but most scholars now doubt the identification because Dublin's name is Irish and Ptolemy's coordinates…

edeco.s: Edeco was a chieftain of the Edetani, an Iberian people of the Valencia region, during the Second Punic War. After Scipio took Carthago Nova in 209 BCE, where the Carthaginians held his wife and children as hostages, Edeco was the first Iberian leader to come over to the…

edeta.s: Edeta was the chief town of the Edetani, an Iberian people, on the hill of Tossal de Sant Miquel above modern Llíria in the province of Valencia. Flourishing between the 5th and 2nd centuries BCE, it has yielded houses, a sanctuary and painted pottery showing warriors, dancers…

egba-united-board-of-management.s: The Egba United Board of Management was a government set up at Abeokuta in 1865 by George William Johnson, a Saro returnee from Sierra Leone, to give the Egba a modern administration able to resist British pressure from Lagos. It collected customs duties, issued regulations…

eichsfeld.s: The Eichsfeld is a hilly historical region in central Germany, now divided between Thuringia and Lower Saxony, around the towns of Heiligenstadt and Duderstadt. Acquired piece by piece by the archbishops of Mainz from the 11th century, it remained their territory until 1802…

ehrenbreitstein-fortress.s: Ehrenbreitstein Fortress stands on a rock above the Rhine opposite Koblenz and the mouth of the Moselle, in Germany. A castle there belonged to the archbishops of Trier from the 11th century and became a stronghold and residence of the electors.

enserune.s: Ensérune is an oppidum, a fortified hilltop settlement, near Nissan-lez-Ensérune between Béziers and Narbonne in southern France. Occupied from about the 6th century BCE to the 1st century CE, it shows a mix of Iberian, Celtic and Greek influences, with Iberian inscriptions,…

el-tintal.s: El Tintal is a large Preclassic Maya city in the Mirador Basin of northern Guatemala, linked to El Mirador by a causeway. It contains large temple pyramids and flourished in the Late Preclassic period, from about 300 BCE to 150 CE, with some later reoccupation in the Classic…

elusa.s: Elusa, modern Eauze in the Gers department of south-western France, was the chief town of the Elusates, an Aquitanian people. Under Rome it grew into a prosperous town and in the late 3rd century became the capital of the province of Novempopulana, and later the seat of an…

elagabal.s: Elagabal was the sun god of Emesa, modern Homs, in Roman Syria, worshipped in the form of a black conical stone in a great temple served by the priestly kings of the Emesene dynasty. The emperor Elagabalus, a hereditary priest of the cult, brought the stone to Rome around 219…

elagabalus.s: Elagabalus was Roman emperor from 218 to 222, born Varius Avitus Bassianus into the priestly family of Emesa and great-nephew of the empress Julia Domna. Raised to power as a teenager by his grandmother Julia Maesa, who claimed he was Caracalla's son, he made his god Elagabal…

emir-abdelkader.s: Emir Abdelkader was an Algerian religious and military leader who led resistance to the French conquest of Algeria from 1832 to 1847. Chosen as emir by the tribes of western Algeria, he built a state with its own administration, taxes and army, and was recognised by France in…

evliya-celebi.s: Evliya Çelebi was an Ottoman traveller and writer from Istanbul who spent some forty years journeying through the Ottoman Empire and neighbouring lands. His ten-volume Seyahatname, or 'Book of Travels', describes cities, monuments, customs and languages from the Balkans and…

eretna.s: Eretna was a Uyghur commander in the service of the Ilkhanate who founded the Eretnid state in central and eastern Anatolia. Serving under the Ilkhanid governor Timurtash, he ruled the province after Ilkhanid power collapsed and declared himself sultan, ruling from Sivas and…

e-abzu.s: The E-abzu, the house of the abzu, was the temple of the god Enki at Eridu in southern Mesopotamia. Excavations in the 1940s found a sequence of some eighteen temples built one on top of another on the same spot, from a small mud-brick shrine of the Ubaid period to a large…

eritrean-liberation-front.s: The Eritrean Liberation Front was a nationalist movement founded in Cairo in 1960 by Eritrean exiles to win independence from Ethiopia. Its fighters under Hamid Idris Awate began the armed struggle in September 1961.

eritrean-liberation-movement.s: The Eritrean Liberation Movement was a clandestine nationalist organisation founded in 1958 among Eritreans in Port Sudan and spread through secret cells of seven members in Eritrea. It opposed Ethiopia's erosion of Eritrea's autonomy under the federation and drew both Muslims…

erythraean-sibyl.s: The Erythraean Sibyl was a legendary prophetess of Apollo associated with Erythrae, an Ionian city on the coast of Asia Minor opposite Chios. Ancient writers counted her among the most famous of the sibyls, and verses ascribed to her circulated widely.

edo-state.s: Edo State is a state in southern Nigeria, created in 1991 from the former Bendel State, with Benin City as its capital. It covers the heartland of the historic Kingdom of Benin and the lands of the Esan, Owan, Etsako and other peoples.

ekpoma.s: Ekpoma is a town in Edo State in southern Nigeria, the headquarters of the Esan West local government area. It was one of the Esan chiefdoms whose rulers, the Enijie, traced their origins to the Kingdom of Benin.

esrefoglu-mosque.s: The Eşrefoğlu Mosque in Beyşehir, central Turkey, was built in 1296–1299 by Süleyman Bey of the Eshrefid beylik. Its prayer hall has a forest of carved cedar columns supporting a flat wooden roof, with painted ceilings, tiled mihrab and carved fittings, and it is among the…

esus.s: Esus was a Gaulish god named by the Roman poet Lucan, together with Teutates and Taranis, as receiving human sacrifice. He appears on the Pillar of the Boatmen, a 1st-century monument from Paris, as a man cutting a tree, and on a relief from Trier.

exmes.s: Exmes is a village in the Orne department of Normandy, north-western France. In the early Middle Ages it was the chief place of the Hiémois, a district whose name derives from it, and the seat of a castle and of the counts of the Hiémois in the 11th century.

etowah-river.s: The Etowah River flows through north-western Georgia, in the United States, and joins the Oostanaula at Rome to form the Coosa River. Its valley was home to the Etowah chiefdom, one of the great Mississippian centres, whose mounds still stand near Cartersville.

eleutherius-exarch.s: Eleutherius was a eunuch official of the Byzantine Empire who served as exarch of Ravenna from 616. He suppressed a revolt at Naples and restored imperial control in Ravenna.

eutychius-exarch.s: Eutychius was the last Byzantine exarch of Ravenna, governing from the late 720s. He struggled to defend imperial Italy against the Lombards, at times seeking help from the popes, while the dispute over Iconoclasm divided Rome and Constantinople.

ezhimala.s: Ezhimala is a coastal hill in the Kannur district of northern Kerala, India, rising from the shore of the Arabian Sea. In Sangam poetry it was the seat of the chief Nannan, and it later gave its name to the Mushika kingdom of northern Kerala, from which the Kolathiri rulers…

ethiopian-peoples-revolutionary-democrat.s: The Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF) was a coalition of ethnic-based parties led by the Tigray People's Liberation Front under Meles Zenawi. Its forces overthrew the Derg regime in May 1991, and it then governed Ethiopia under the ethnic federal…

epsom-derby.s: The Epsom Derby is a flat horse race for three-year-old colts and fillies run each year over about a mile and a half at Epsom Downs in Surrey, England. First run in 1780 and named after the 12th Earl of Derby, it is the most prestigious race of the British flat season.

eurico-gaspar-dutra.s: Eurico Gaspar Dutra was a Brazilian general who served as Getúlio Vargas's war minister from 1936 to 1945, supporting the Estado Novo dictatorship, and then joined the officers who removed Vargas in 1945. Elected president that year, he governed from 1946 to 1951 under the new…

esslingen-am-neckar.s: Esslingen am Neckar is a city near Stuttgart in Baden-Württemberg that grew around a shrine of Saint Vitalis and a bridge over the Neckar. A free imperial city from the 13th century until 1802, it was a leading member of the Swabian city leagues, and the Swabian League was…

elijah-levita.s: Elijah Levita was a Hebrew grammarian, scholar and Yiddish poet born near Nuremberg who spent most of his life in Italy. He taught Hebrew to Christian humanists, among them Cardinal Egidio da Viterbo, and around 1540 worked with Paul Fagius at a Hebrew press in Isny.

erfurt.s: Erfurt is the capital of the German state of Thuringia, a city on the Gera first recorded in 742, when Saint Boniface founded a short-lived bishopric there. In the Middle Ages it was the richest city of Thuringia, trading in woad, and kept wide self-government under the…

eugen-bolz.s: Eugen Bolz was a German Catholic Centre Party politician who was state president of Württemberg from 1928 until the Nazis removed him in 1933. Linked to the resistance circle of Carl Goerdeler, he was to have been a minister in the government planned after the 20 July plot of…

edouard-bremond.s: Édouard Brémond was a French army officer. During the First World War he led the French military mission to the Hejaz, which supported the Arab Revolt, and from 1919 to 1920 he was chief administrator of the French-occupied zone of Cilicia, relying partly on the Armenian Legion.

ecole-william-ponty.s: The École William Ponty was a teacher-training college in French West Africa, founded at Saint-Louis in Senegal in 1903, moved to Gorée in 1913 and later to Sébikotane. Named after the governor-general William Merlaud-Ponty, it trained African teachers, clerks and medical…

ems.s: The Ems is a river of north-western Germany, about 370 km long, rising in the Senne near Paderborn and flowing north through Westphalia and Lower Saxony to the Dollart estuary and the North Sea near Emden. In Roman times the Bructeri, Frisii and Chauci lived along it, and in…

ensisheim.s: Ensisheim is a small town in Alsace, France, north of Mulhouse. From the late 15th century until the Thirty Years' War it was the seat of the Habsburg government of Further Austria, with a regency and treasury for the western lands.

elberfeld.s: Elberfeld is a former town in the Wupper valley of western Germany, joined with Barmen and neighbouring towns in 1929 to form the city later named Wuppertal. A centre of linen bleaching and then of textiles and dyeing from the sixteenth century, it was one of the first…

elias-lonnrot.s: Elias Lönnrot was a Finnish physician and philologist who collected oral folk poetry on long journeys through Finland and Karelia and compiled from it the national epic, the Kalevala, published in 1835 and enlarged in 1849. He also compiled a great Finnish–Swedish dictionary…

eduard-flottwell.s: Eduard Heinrich Flottwell was a Prussian administrator who served as president of the Grand Duchy of Posen from 1830 to 1841. After the November Uprising he pursued a policy of Germanisation, restricting Polish in the administration, buying up Polish noble estates for German…

eudokia-dmitriyevna.s: Eudokia Dmitriyevna was Grand Princess of Moscow as the wife of Dmitry Donskoy, whom she married in 1366. A daughter of Dmitry Konstantinovich of Suzdal and Nizhny Novgorod, she sealed the alliance between the two princely houses.

evpaty-kolovrat.s: Evpaty Kolovrat is a legendary Ryazan noble whose deeds are told in the Tale of the Destruction of Ryazan by Batu, a work of Old Russian literature. Returning from Chernigov after the Mongols destroyed Ryazan in December 1237, he is said to have gathered some 1,700 men and…

elias-peter-hoayek.s: Elias Peter Hoayek was Maronite Patriarch of Antioch from 1898 to 1931. He led a Lebanese delegation to the Paris Peace Conference in 1919, asking for an independent Lebanon enlarged beyond Mount Lebanon under French protection.

eucratides-i.s: Eucratides I was a Greco-Bactrian king who seized power around 170 BCE, overthrowing the Euthydemid dynasty and fighting the Indo-Greek kings south of the Hindu Kush. He issued some of the finest Hellenistic coins, including the largest gold coin of antiquity, a twenty-stater…

euthydemus-i.s: Euthydemus I was a Greco-Bactrian king from Magnesia who overthrew Diodotus II around 225 BCE and founded the Euthydemid dynasty. He withstood a two-year siege of Bactra by the Seleucid king Antiochus III, who in about 206 BCE recognised him as king and offered a daughter in…

ermanaric.s: Ermanaric was a king of the Greuthungi Goths in the 4th century, ruling lands north of the Black Sea. Ammianus Marcellinus describes him as a warlike king who took his own life when the Huns attacked around 375, while Jordanes later credited him with a vast realm.

erridupizir.s: Erridupizir was a Gutian king who ruled in Mesopotamia in the 22nd century BCE, after the fall of the Akkadian Empire. He is known from copies of his inscriptions found at Nippur, in which he took the Akkadian title 'king of the four quarters' and recorded campaigns in the…

erasmus.s: Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam was a Dutch humanist scholar, the most famous of the Northern Renaissance. His Greek edition of the New Testament of 1516, his satire The Praise of Folly and his many letters and editions of the Church Fathers made him a leading voice for reform…

el-escorial.s: El Escorial is a vast royal monastery and palace north-west of Madrid, built for Philip II of Spain between 1563 and 1584. Designed by Juan Bautista de Toledo and Juan de Herrera, it combines a monastery, basilica, royal palace, library and burial place of the Spanish kings in…

eleni-of-ethiopia.s: Eleni was an Ethiopian empress, born a princess of the Muslim Hadiya Sultanate, who married Emperor Zara Yaqob and converted to Christianity. She remained a powerful figure at court under several later emperors and acted as regent for the young Lebna Dengel.

ecija.s: Écija is a town in the province of Seville in Andalusia, Spain, on the Genil river. As the Roman colony of Astigi it was an important centre of olive oil production, and it was a bishopric under the Visigoths.

egirdir.s: Eğirdir is a town in Isparta province, south-western Turkey, on the southern shore of Lake Eğirdir. In the 14th century it was the first capital of the Hamidid beylik, and its Seljuk caravanserai, converted into the Dündar Bey madrasa, survives from that period.

essenes.s: The Essenes were a Jewish religious movement of the Second Temple period, active from about the 2nd century BCE to the 1st century CE. Described by Josephus, Philo and Pliny the Elder, they lived communally, shared their property and practised strict ritual purity.

emil-von-zelewski.s: Emil von Zelewski was a German officer who commanded the colonial troops in German East Africa. In August 1891 he led an expedition against the Hehe chief Mkwawa and was killed with most of his column in an ambush at Lugalo near Iringa, one of the worst defeats suffered by…

eurybiades.s: Eurybiades was the Spartan admiral who commanded the allied Greek fleet during Xerxes' invasion of Greece in 480 BCE. Although the Athenian contingent was by far the largest, the allies insisted on a Spartan commander.

ezo.s: Ezo was the Japanese name for the lands north of Honshu inhabited by the Ainu, especially the island now called Hokkaido. From the 16th century the Matsumae clan controlled its southern tip and the Ainu trade, while the shogunate took direct control at times of Russian pressure.

ethiopian-red-terror.s: The Ethiopian Red Terror was a campaign of violent repression waged by the Derg military government under Mengistu Haile Mariam, at its height in 1977-1978. Aimed chiefly at the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Party and other leftist rivals, it involved mass arrests, torture…

etelkoz.s: Etelköz was the land between the Dnieper and the lower Danube, north of the Black Sea, where the Hungarians lived in the 9th century before their conquest of the Carpathian Basin. It is named in Constantine VII's De Administrando Imperio.

ekiti-people.s: The Ekiti are a Yoruba subgroup of south-western Nigeria, living in hilly country now forming Ekiti State. Organised in many small kingdoms, they were dominated by Ibadan from the mid-19th century.

edda.s: Edda is the name of two medieval Icelandic works that preserve Old Norse myth and heroic legend. The Prose Edda, written by Snorri Sturluson around 1220, is a handbook of poetics and mythology, while the Poetic Edda is a collection of older anonymous poems known mainly from a…

epirus.s: Epirus is a mountainous region of south-eastern Europe between the Pindus range and the Ionian Sea, divided today between north-western Greece and southern Albania. In antiquity it was home to the Molossians and other Greek-speaking tribes, whose kingdom reached its height…

elchingen.s: Elchingen is a municipality in the district of Neu-Ulm in Bavaria, Germany, on the Danube north-east of Ulm. Its village of Oberelchingen grew up around the Benedictine Imperial Abbey of Elchingen, founded in the 12th century, whose rebuilt church survives.

engelberg.s: Engelberg is a village and mountain resort in the canton of Obwalden in central Switzerland, lying in a high valley below Titlis. It grew around the Benedictine abbey founded in 1120, whose abbots ruled the valley as a small independent territory until 1798.

essen-cathedral.s: Essen Cathedral is the cathedral of the Roman Catholic diocese of Essen in the Ruhr, Germany. It was built as the church of Essen Abbey, a community of noble canonesses founded in the 9th century, and keeps its Ottonian westwork and a Gothic hall church.

elisabeth-of-the-palatinate.s: Elisabeth of the Palatinate was a German princess and philosopher, the eldest daughter of Frederick V, the 'Winter King' of Bohemia. Raised in exile in the Netherlands, she carried on a celebrated correspondence with René Descartes from 1643 on the relation of mind and body,…

essen.s: Essen is a city in the Ruhr in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. It grew around Essen Abbey, a community of noble canonesses founded in the 9th century whose princess-abbesses ruled the town until 1803.

emporda.s: The Empordà is a region of north-eastern Catalonia in Spain, between the Pyrenees and the Mediterranean, now divided into Alt Empordà and Baix Empordà. It takes its name from the Greek colony of Emporion, later Roman Emporiae, at Empúries on its coast.

eidagale.s: The Eidagale are a Somali clan, a subdivision of the Isaaq, living mainly around Hargeisa and in the west of Somaliland. The Isaaq Sultanate's ruling house, the Rer Guled, came from the Eidagale, and its first sultan, Guled Abdi, was chosen in the 18th century.

enlil-bani.s: Enlil-bani was a king of the Isin dynasty in Mesopotamia in the 19th century BCE. Later Babylonian chronicles tell that he was a gardener installed by King Erra-imitti as a substitute king to avert an evil omen; when Erra-imitti died suddenly, Enlil-bani kept the throne.

erra-imitti.s: Erra-imitti was a king of the Isin dynasty in Mesopotamia in the 19th century BCE, a time when Isin was losing ground to Larsa. He is best remembered from a later Babylonian chronicle, which says that he placed the gardener Enlil-bani on the throne as a substitute king and…

elazig.s: Elazığ is a city in eastern Anatolia, Turkey, on a plain east of the Euphrates. It was founded in the 19th century below the old fortress town of Harput and named Mamuret-ul-Aziz after Sultan Abdulaziz.

eoganachta.s: The Eóganachta were a group of related dynasties that ruled the Kingdom of Munster in early medieval Ireland, claiming descent from Éogan Mór. From about the 5th century their branches, such as the Eóganacht Chaisil around Cashel and the Eóganacht Locha Léin in the west,…

emperor-aizong-of-jin.s: Emperor Aizong was the ninth emperor of the Jurchen Jin dynasty, ruling from 1224 to 1234. Facing the Mongols, he ended the wars with Western Xia and the Song, but in 1232 the Mongols overran Henan and besieged Kaifeng.

emperor-taizu-of-jin.s: Wanyan Aguda was the founder of the Jurchen Jin dynasty and its first emperor, known as Taizu, ruling from 1115 to 1123. Chief of the Wanyan clan in Manchuria, he rebelled against the Khitan Liao dynasty in 1114, proclaimed the Jin in 1115 and won a series of victories that…

enzo-of-sardinia.s: Enzo was an illegitimate son of Emperor Frederick II who became King of Sardinia by title after marrying Adelasia of Torres in 1238. He served his father as imperial vicar in Italy, but was captured by Bologna at the Battle of Fossalta in 1249.

elephanta-caves.s: The Elephanta Caves are rock-cut cave temples on Elephanta Island in Mumbai harbour, India, mostly dedicated to Shiva and carved in the 5th to 6th centuries. The main cave holds a huge three-headed image of Shiva, the Sadashiva.

ellora-caves.s: The Ellora Caves are a group of 34 rock-cut Buddhist, Hindu and Jain temples and monasteries near Aurangabad in Maharashtra, India, carved between about 600 and 1000 CE. The most famous, the Kailasa temple, was cut from a single mass of rock under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna…

engelbrekt-engelbrektsson.s: Engelbrekt Engelbrektsson was a Swedish mine owner from the Bergslagen mining district who led a rebellion in 1434 against King Eric of Pomerania and his Danish bailiffs. Supported by miners, peasants and later nobles, the revolt spread across Sweden and he was chosen as…

eikyo-rebellion.s: The Eikyō Rebellion was a revolt in 1438 and 1439 by Ashikaga Mochiuji, governor-general of the Kanto at Kamakura, against the shogun Ashikaga Yoshinori in Kyoto. Mochiuji had long defied the shogunate and fallen out with his deputy, Uesugi Norizane, who sided with the shogun.

emperor-go-toba.s: Go-Toba was emperor of Japan from 1183 to 1198 and then ruled as retired emperor. Seeking to restore imperial power, he raised forces against the Kamakura shogunate in the Jokyu War of 1221 but was defeated by the Hojo regents and exiled to the Oki Islands, where he died.

el-chayal.s: El Chayal is an obsidian source in the highlands north-east of Guatemala City. From early times its volcanic glass was quarried and traded widely across the Maya region for blades and tools.

evrenos-bey.s: Evrenos Bey was a Turkish frontier commander who, after serving the beylik of Karesi, became one of the leading Ottoman marcher lords in the Balkans. From the 1360s he led raids and conquests in Thrace, Macedonia and Greece, and founded Giannitsa (Yenice-i Vardar), where his…

enlil-nadin-ahi.s: Enlil-nadin-ahi was the last king of the Kassite dynasty of Babylonia, ruling for about three years in the mid-12th century BCE. Elamite armies under Shutruk-Nahhunte and his son Kutir-Nahhunte invaded Babylonia, and he was carried off to Elam around 1155 BCE.

evelyn-baring-1st-baron-howick-of-glenda.n: Evelyn Baring, 1st Baron Howick of Glendale
evelyn-baring-1st-baron-howick-of-glenda.s: Evelyn Baring, later 1st Baron Howick of Glendale, was a British colonial administrator and governor of Kenya from 1952 to 1959. Soon after arriving he declared a state of emergency against the Mau Mau uprising, which led to mass detention of Kikuyu and the hanging of more…

elkab.s: Elkab, ancient Nekheb, is an archaeological site on the east bank of the Nile in Upper Egypt, south of Luxor. It was the cult centre of the vulture goddess Nekhbet, patron of Upper Egypt.

evelyn-baring-1st-earl-of-cromer.s: Evelyn Baring, 1st Earl of Cromer, was a British administrator who, as agent and consul-general in Egypt from 1883 to 1907, was the effective ruler of the country under the British occupation. He restored Egypt's finances and expanded irrigation, but opposed nationalist…

enkomi.s: Enkomi is an archaeological site near Famagusta on the east coast of Cyprus, one of the chief towns of the island in the Late Bronze Age. It had a harbour, copper workshops and ashlar buildings, and its finds include the bronze statue known as the Horned God and Cypro-Minoan…

eteocypriot-language.s: Eteocypriot is the name given to a non-Greek language of ancient Cyprus, known from inscriptions written in the Cypriot syllabary between about the 8th and 4th centuries BCE. Most texts come from Amathus, whose people ancient writers regarded as descendants of the island's…

etchmiadzin-cathedral.s: Etchmiadzin Cathedral, in the city of Vagharshapat in Armenia, is the mother church of the Armenian Apostolic Church and the seat of its Catholicos. Tradition says Gregory the Illuminator built it after a vision soon after Armenia adopted Christianity in the early 4th century,…

erediauwa.s: Erediauwa was the Oba of Benin from 1979 until his death in 2016. Born Solomon Igbinoghodua Akenzua, the son of Oba Akenzua II, he studied at Cambridge and served as a senior civil servant in Nigeria before succeeding to the throne.

elisedd-ap-gwylog.s: Elisedd ap Gwylog was a king of Powys in the first half of the 8th century. He is known chiefly from the Pillar of Eliseg near Llangollen, erected by his great-grandson Cyngen ap Cadell, whose inscription records that Elisedd won back land from the English with fire and sword.

epyaxa.s: Epyaxa was queen of Cilicia, the wife of its king Syennesis, in the late 5th century BCE. According to Xenophon's Anabasis, she met Cyrus the Younger in 401 BCE during his march against his brother Artaxerxes II, gave him money to pay his troops and watched a review of his army.

ershi.s: Ershi was the capital of Dayuan, the kingdom of the Ferghana valley in Central Asia known to Han China for its 'heavenly horses'. In 102 BCE the Han general Li Guangli besieged it and cut off its water supply until the nobles killed their king and agreed to hand over horses.

easter-controversy.s: The Easter controversy was a long dispute in the early medieval Church over how to calculate the date of Easter. In Britain and Ireland the native churches kept an older reckoning, while Roman missionaries and their supporters pressed for the system used at Rome.

eifionydd.s: Eifionydd is a historic district in north-west Wales, between Snowdonia and Tremadog Bay at the root of the Llŷn peninsula. With Ardudwy it made up the early kingdom of Dunoding, and it later became a commote of Gwynedd centred on Criccieth.

ely-cambridgeshire.s: Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire, England, on a former island in the Fens. Æthelthryth founded a monastery there in 673; refounded in 970, it became a cathedral in 1109, and its Romanesque and Gothic cathedral dominates the flat landscape. Hereward the Wake held out…

el-alamein.s: El Alamein is a town on Egypt's Mediterranean coast, about 100 kilometres west of Alexandria. In 1942 it gave its name to two battles of the Second World War: in July the British Eighth Army halted the Axis advance on Egypt there, and in October and November Montgomery's…

ely-ocarroll.s: Ely O'Carroll was a Gaelic lordship in the Irish midlands, covering much of what is now south County Offaly and north County Tipperary around Birr. It took its name from the ancient kingdom of Éile and from the O'Carrolls who ruled it from the 11th century until the 16th.

enniskillen.s: Enniskillen is the county town of Fermanagh in Northern Ireland, on an island between Upper and Lower Lough Erne. Growing around the 15th-century castle of the Maguires, it became a plantation town and Protestant garrison in the 17th century and held out for William III in 1689.

enniskillen-castle.s: Enniskillen Castle is a castle in Enniskillen, County Fermanagh, built by the Maguire lords of Fermanagh in the 15th century to guard the passage between Upper and Lower Lough Erne. Taken by the English in 1594 and rebuilt in the 17th century, it later served as a barracks and…

eoganan-mac-oengusa.s: Eóganán mac Óengusa was king of the Picts and of Fortriu from about 837, a son of Óengus II. In 839 he was killed with his brother Bran and many nobles in a great battle against the Vikings.

edict-of-nantes.s: The Edict of Nantes was issued by Henry IV of France in April 1598 to end the French Wars of Religion. It granted the Protestant Huguenots freedom of conscience, rights of worship in defined places, civil equality and fortified towns as security.

estates-general-france.s: The Estates General was the assembly of the three orders of the Kingdom of France, clergy, nobility and commoners, first summoned by Philip IV in 1302. It met irregularly to grant taxes or advise the crown and was not called between 1614 and 1789.

eoganacht-raithlind.s: The Eóganacht Raithlind were a branch of the Eóganacht dynasties of Munster, based in the south of the province around Cork and the Bandon valley, who at times held the kingship of Munster in the early Middle Ages. Their Uí Echach line became the O'Mahonys, while the Uí…

elijah.s: Elijah was a Hebrew prophet of the 9th century BCE in the northern Kingdom of Israel, known from the biblical Books of Kings. He opposed King Ahab and Queen Jezebel and their promotion of the worship of Baal, most famously in the contest on Mount Carmel, and was said to have…

eadberht-praen.s: Eadberht Præn was king of Kent from 796 to 798, leading a revolt against Mercian rule after the death of Offa. A former cleric, he seized the throne and drove out Archbishop Æthelheard of Canterbury, but in 798 Coenwulf of Mercia invaded Kent, captured him, had him blinded and…

egbert-of-wessex.s: Egbert was king of Wessex from 802 to 839. After defeating Beornwulf of Mercia at the Battle of Ellendun in 825, he took Kent, Surrey, Sussex and Essex, and in 829 he briefly conquered Mercia itself and received the submission of Northumbria, so that the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle…

essau.s: Essau is a town on the north bank of the Gambia River in the North Bank Region of The Gambia, opposite Banjul. It was a royal seat of the Mandinka kingdom of Niumi, whose kings were chosen in rotation from royal lineages in several towns.

etosha-pan.s: Etosha Pan is a large salt pan in northern Namibia, about 120 km long, which fills with water only briefly after heavy rains. Ovambo peoples collected salt there and traded it widely.

eumenes-i.s: Eumenes I was ruler of Pergamon from 263 to 241 BCE, the nephew and adopted heir of Philetaerus. He defeated the Seleucid king Antiochus I near Sardis around 261 BCE, making Pergamon independent and extending its territory, though he never took the title king.

evelthon.s: Evelthon was king of Salamis in Cyprus in the 6th century BCE. He is credited with some of the island's earliest coins and, according to Herodotus, dedicated a censer at Delphi and refused Pheretime of Cyrene an army, giving her instead a golden spindle and distaff.

eunostos-of-soloi.s: Eunostos was the last king of Soloi in Cyprus, ruling at the end of the 4th century BCE as an ally of Ptolemy I. He married Eirene, a daughter of Ptolemy, which bound his small kingdom to the Ptolemaic dynasty.

expo-92.s: Expo '92 was a world's fair held in Seville, Spain, from 20 April to 12 October 1992, marking the 500th anniversary of Columbus's first voyage to the Americas. Built on the island of La Cartuja, it received more than 40 million visits and brought major investment, including…

eorcenwald.s: Eorcenwald was Bishop of London from 675 until his death around 693 and a founder of monasteries in south-east England. Before becoming bishop he founded Chertsey Abbey and, for his sister Æthelburh, Barking Abbey.

edict-of-rothari.s: The Edict of Rothari was the first written law code of the Lombards, issued by King Rothari at Pavia in November 643. Written in Latin, its 388 chapters set out Lombard customary law, including fixed money compensation for injuries in place of blood feud.

eugippius.s: Eugippius was a monk and disciple of Saint Severinus, who left Noricum with the Roman population in 488 and became abbot of a monastery near Naples. Around 511 he wrote the Life of Saint Severinus, a vivid account of the last years of Roman rule on the Danube.

ennis.s: Ennis is the county town of County Clare in the west of Ireland, on the River Fergus. It grew around a Franciscan friary founded by the O'Brien kings of Thomond in the 13th century, near their seat at Clonroad.

eogan-mac-neill.s: Eógan mac Néill is the traditional ancestor of the Cenél nEógain, one of the sons of Niall of the Nine Hostages in Irish genealogy, said to have died in 465. Tír Eoghain, Eógan's land, now Tyrone, and Inishowen were named after him.

eurystheus.s: Eurystheus is a figure of Greek mythology, king of Tiryns and Mycenae and a descendant of Perseus. According to the myths, Hera arranged his early birth so that he, not Heracles, would rule, and he imposed the Twelve Labours on Heracles.

epic-of-kirta.s: The Epic of Kirta is a poem from Ugarit preserved on three clay tablets in alphabetic cuneiform. It tells of King Kirta, who loses his family, is told by the god El in a dream to win a new bride by force, and later falls ill after breaking a vow.

erebuni.s: Erebuni is an Urartian fortress on the Arin Berd hill in the south-east of Yerevan, Armenia. A cuneiform inscription records its founding by King Argishti I in 782 BCE, and it served as an Urartian administrative and military centre in the Ararat plain.

epic-of-manas.s: The Epic of Manas is the traditional oral epic of the Kyrgyz, telling of the hero Manas, his son Semetey and grandson Seytek, who unite the Kyrgyz and fight their enemies. Performed by reciters called manaschi, it is among the longest epics in the world, with some versions…

eudoxus-of-cnidus.s: Eudoxus of Cnidus was a Greek mathematician and astronomer of the 4th century BCE. He developed a theory of proportion and the method of exhaustion, later used in Euclid's Elements, and devised the first geometrical model of the motions of the planets, a system of nested…

epimenides.s: Epimenides was a semi-legendary Cretan seer and poet, traditionally dated to the 7th or 6th century BCE. Greek tradition says he purified Athens of the pollution caused by the killing of the followers of Cylon, and stories told of his sleep of fifty-seven years in a cave.

ernest-de-sarzec.s: Ernest de Sarzec was a French diplomat and archaeologist who, as vice-consul at Basra, excavated the mound of Telloh in southern Iraq from 1877. His finds, including statues of Gudea, the Gudea Cylinders and the Stele of the Vultures, revealed the Sumerian civilisation of…

eisenach.s: Eisenach is a town in western Thuringia, Germany, at the edge of the Thuringian Forest, below the Wartburg castle. It was a residence of the Ludowingian landgraves of Thuringia and later the capital of the Duchy of Saxe-Eisenach.

elizabeth-of-hungary.s: Elizabeth of Hungary was a daughter of King Andrew II of Hungary and Gertrude of Merania who married Landgrave Louis IV of Thuringia. After his death on crusade in 1227 she left the Wartburg court, founded a hospital at Marburg and devoted herself to the poor and sick under…

elizabeth-of-pomerania.s: Elizabeth of Pomerania was the daughter of Duke Bogislaw V of Pomerania and granddaughter of King Casimir III of Poland. In 1363 she became the fourth wife of Emperor Charles IV and was crowned Queen of Bohemia and Holy Roman Empress.

e-babbar.s: The E-babbar, 'white house' in Sumerian, was the name of the temples of the sun god Utu, called Shamash in Akkadian, at Larsa and at Sippar in Mesopotamia. Both were among the oldest and most important sanctuaries of Babylonia and were rebuilt by many kings, including…

el-castillo-chichen-itza.s: El Castillo, also called the Temple of Kukulcán, is a step pyramid at the centre of the Maya city of Chichén Itzá in Yucatán, Mexico, built between about the 9th and 12th centuries. It has four stairways and nine terraces, and at the equinoxes the afternoon sun casts a shadow…

emperor-taizu-of-liao.s: Yelü Abaoji, Emperor Taizu of Liao, was the Khitan leader who founded the Liao dynasty. Chosen as khagan around 907, he broke with the custom of rotating leadership, proclaimed himself emperor in 916 and built a state combining steppe and Chinese institutions, including a…

emperor-tianzuo-of-liao.s: Emperor Tianzuo (Yelü Yanxi) was the ninth and last emperor of the Liao dynasty, reigning from 1101 to 1125. His failure to deal with the Jurchen rising led by Aguda in 1114 brought defeat after defeat, and he fled into the western steppe as the Jin took his capitals.

epponina.s: Epponina was the wife of Julius Sabinus, a Lingonian nobleman who rebelled against Rome in 70 CE. She hid him in an underground refuge for nine years and bore two sons there.

emperor-xiaowu-of-liu-song.s: Emperor Xiaowu (Liu Jun) was the fourth emperor of the Liu Song dynasty in southern China, reigning from 453 to 464. He came to the throne after defeating his elder brother Liu Shao, who had murdered their father, Emperor Wen.

emperor-xiaowu-of-northern-wei.s: Emperor Xiaowu (Yuan Xiu) was the last emperor of the undivided Northern Wei, placed on the throne in 532 by the general Gao Huan. In 534 he fled from Gao Huan's control at Luoyang to the general Yuwen Tai at Chang'an, who had him poisoned early in 535.

edward-ii-of-england.s: Edward II was king of England from 1307 to 1327, the son of Edward I. His reliance on favourites such as Piers Gaveston and the Despensers alienated the barons, and his army was routed by Robert the Bruce at Bannockburn in 1314.

edward-stafford-3rd-duke-of-buckingham.s: Edward Stafford, 3rd Duke of Buckingham, was one of the greatest English nobles of the early Tudor period, a descendant of Edward III with large estates in England and the Welsh Marches, including Brecknock. His royal blood and hostility to Cardinal Wolsey made Henry VIII…

englishry.s: The Englishry was the lowland part of a marcher lordship in Wales, settled by English and Flemish colonists and run under English law and manorial custom, as distinct from the upland Welshry, where Welsh tenants kept Welsh law and customs. The division was clearest in…

eudokia-angelina.s: Eudokia Angelina was a daughter of the Byzantine emperor Alexios III Angelos. She was first married to the Serbian prince Stefan Nemanjić and, after their separation, to Alexios V Doukas, briefly emperor during the Fourth Crusade.

eudokia-palaiologina.s: Eudokia Palaiologina was a daughter of the Byzantine emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos who married Emperor John II of Trebizond in 1282. The marriage brought Trebizond closer to Constantinople, and John gave up the title of emperor of the Romans.

earl-of-derby.s: Earl of Derby is a title in the peerage of England held since 1485 by the Stanley family. Thomas Stanley received it from Henry VII after the Battle of Bosworth, and his heirs were also Lords of Mann until 1736.

eschen.s: Eschen is a municipality in the Unterland of Liechtenstein, on the slopes of the Eschnerberg. In the Middle Ages and early modern period it belonged to the Lordship of Schellenberg, which was united with the County of Vaduz in 1719 to form the Principality of Liechtenstein.

eschnerberg.s: The Eschnerberg is a low, wooded ridge in the Unterland of Liechtenstein, rising above the Rhine valley. Inhabited since the Neolithic, it carried the castles of the Schellenberg family in the 13th century, and villages of the former Lordship of Schellenberg, such as Eschen,…

edward-iv-of-england.s: Edward IV was King of England from 1461 to 1470 and again from 1471 to 1483, the first Yorkist king. He won the throne in the Wars of the Roses with victories at Mortimer's Cross and Towton, lost it briefly to the restored Henry VI, and regained it at Barnet and Tewkesbury.

exobourgo.s: Exobourgo is a granite hill about 640 metres high in the centre of the island of Tinos in the Cyclades, Greece. A fortified town stood on its summit from the 13th century under the Ghisi family and then Venice, protecting the islanders from pirates and Ottoman raids.

eulalia-of-merida.s: Eulalia of Mérida was a young Christian martyred at Emerita Augusta, capital of Roman Lusitania, in 304 during the persecution of Diocletian. The poet Prudentius celebrated her death in his hymns, and her cult spread widely across Hispania and beyond.

endovelicus.s: Endovelicus was a god of the pre-Roman peoples of western Iberia, worshipped above all at a sanctuary near Alandroal in Portugal's Alentejo. Dozens of Latin dedications from the Roman period, many by people with Roman names, thank him for health or answered prayers, suggesting…

edward-gent.s: Sir Edward Gent was a British colonial official who served as governor of the Malayan Union from 1946 to 1948 and then as the first high commissioner of the Federation of Malaya. He had helped plan the union, which met strong Malay opposition and was replaced by the federation…

edict-of-worms.s: The Edict of Worms was a decree issued by the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V on 25 May 1521, at the close of the Diet of Worms, declaring Martin Luther an outlaw and a heretic. It ordered his arrest, banned the reading and possession of his writings, and forbade anyone to…

emancipation-proclamation.s: The Emancipation Proclamation was an executive order issued by President Abraham Lincoln on 1 January 1863, during the American Civil War, declaring free all enslaved people in the states then in rebellion against the Union. It did not apply to the slave states loyal to the…

emmeline-pankhurst.s: Emmeline Pankhurst was a British political activist who led the militant campaign for women's suffrage. In 1903 she founded the Women's Social and Political Union, whose members, the suffragettes, turned from processions and heckling to window-smashing and arson, and she was…

equal-franchise-act-1928.s: The Representation of the People (Equal Franchise) Act 1928 gave women in the United Kingdom the vote on the same terms as men, from the age of twenty-one. It extended the franchise granted in 1918 to women over thirty who met a property qualification, adding some five million…

emmendingen.s: Emmendingen is a town in Baden-Württemberg, Germany, north of Freiburg in the Breisgau. Near it stand the ruins of the Hochburg, the castle of the margraves of Hachberg, and the town was later an administrative seat of the margraves of Baden.

eisenerz.s: Eisenerz is a mining town in Styria, Austria, at the foot of the Erzberg, the 'iron ore mountain'. Iron ore has been mined there since the Middle Ages, and the town grew rich supplying the iron trade of Styria and Upper Austria.

enns-river.s: The Enns is a river about 250 kilometres long in Austria, rising in the Radstadt Tauern in Salzburg and flowing through Styria to join the Danube at the town of Enns. For centuries it formed the boundary between Upper and Lower Austria, which were long called Austria above and…

erzberg.s: The Erzberg is a mountain near Eisenerz in Styria, Austria, made largely of siderite iron ore and mined since at least the Middle Ages. Open-cast mining has cut it into giant terraces, giving it the look of a stepped pyramid.

east-khasi-hills.s: East Khasi Hills is a district of Meghalaya in north-eastern India, containing the state capital, Shillong. It covers part of the Khasi Hills plateau, home of the Khasi people, whose small chiefdoms, headed by syiems, came under British supervision in the nineteenth century…

erzincan.s: Erzincan is a city in eastern Turkey on the upper Euphrates, in a fertile plain surrounded by mountains. In the Middle Ages it was the seat of the Mengujekid emirs and later of the Eretnids and local emirs before passing to the Ottomans.

egnatia.s: Egnatia, or Gnathia, was an ancient city on the Adriatic coast of Apulia, southern Italy, between Bari and Brindisi. A Messapian town, it later became a Roman municipium on the Via Traiana and gave its name to Gnathia ware, a type of painted pottery of the fourth and third…

ennius.s: Quintus Ennius was a Latin poet, born in 239 BCE at Rudiae in the Messapian south of Italy. Brought to Rome by Cato, he wrote tragedies, comedies and satires, and his epic Annales, telling the history of Rome in hexameters, made him known as the father of Latin poetry.

el-nino.s: El Niño is the periodic warming of surface waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific, part of a climate cycle that recurs every few years. On the coast of Peru it brings torrential rains and floods to normally dry deserts and drives away fish from cold upwelling waters.

esen-buqa-ii.s: Esen Buqa II was khan of Moghulistan from about 1429 until his death in 1462. He ruled the eastern part of the khanate while his elder brother Yunus Khan, backed by the Timurids, contested the throne in the west.

eryx.s: Eryx was an ancient Elymian city on Mount Eryx in western Sicily, on the site of modern Erice. It was famous for its sanctuary of a fertility goddess, identified by Greeks with Aphrodite and by Romans with Venus Erycina, whose cult drew sailors from across the Mediterranean.

eurotas.s: The Eurotas is the main river of Laconia in the southern Peloponnese, Greece, flowing past Sparta into the Laconian Gulf. Its fertile valley was the heart of the Mycenaean kingdom remembered as that of Menelaus and later of the Spartan state.

euboea.s: Euboea is the second-largest Greek island, lying along the east coast of central Greece and separated from the mainland by the narrow Euripus strait. Its cities of Chalcis and Eretria led early Greek colonisation in the 8th century BCE, founding settlements in Italy, Sicily…

el-atteuf.s: El Atteuf is the oldest of the five fortified towns of the Mzab valley in the Algerian Sahara, founded by Ibadi Berbers around 1012. Its houses climb a hill around the mosque in the compact style of the valley.

emerald-mound.s: Emerald Mound is a large Mississippian-period platform mound near Natchez, Mississippi, in the United States, built from about 1250 by ancestors of the Natchez people. Covering about 3 hectares, it is one of the largest such mounds in North America, an earthen platform topped…

espiritu-pampa.s: Espíritu Pampa is an archaeological site in the forested lowlands of the Cusco region of Peru, identified as Vilcabamba, the last refuge of the Neo-Inca State. The Inca rulers held out there against the Spanish until 1572, when an expedition captured Túpac Amaru.

ebroin.s: Ebroin was mayor of the palace of Neustria, the western Frankish kingdom, from about 658 until his murder around 681. Ruling in the names of Merovingian kings, he fought the aristocracies of Burgundy and Austrasia and had his opponent Bishop Leodegar of Autun blinded and later…

esperanto.s: Esperanto is a constructed international language created by the Polish ophthalmologist L. L.

edward-whalley.s: Edward Whalley was an English Parliamentarian cavalry commander in the Civil War, a cousin of Oliver Cromwell, and one of the judges who signed the death warrant of Charles I in 1649. At the Restoration in 1660 he fled to New England with his son-in-law William Goffe.

espiritu-santo.s: Espiritu Santo is the largest island of Vanuatu, in the south-west Pacific; its main town is Luganville. It was named by the navigator Pedro Fernandes de Queirós, who landed there in 1606 believing he had found the great southern continent.

ekur.s: The Ekur, Sumerian for 'mountain house', was the temple of the god Enlil at Nippur in Mesopotamia and the most important religious centre of Sumer. Because Enlil was held to grant kingship, rulers of Kish, Uruk, Ur, Akkad and later Babylon sought recognition there and rebuilt…

edigu.s: Edigu was an emir of the Mangit tribe who, though not a descendant of Genghis Khan, dominated the Golden Horde from about 1396 to 1411 through puppet khans. He defeated Vytautas of Lithuania and the former khan Tokhtamysh at the Battle of the Vorskla River in 1399 and besieged…

emperor-komyo.s: Emperor Kōmyō was the second emperor of the Northern Court of Japan, reigning from 1336 to 1348. A member of the Jimyōin line, he was placed on the throne in Kyoto by Ashikaga Takauji after Emperor Go-Daigo broke with the Ashikaga and fled to Yoshino, opening the period of the…

emperor-suko.s: Emperor Sukō was the third emperor of the Northern Court of Japan, reigning from 1348 to 1351, a son of Emperor Kōgon. He was deposed when Ashikaga Takauji briefly submitted to the Southern Court, and in 1352 Southern forces carried him off with the retired emperors Kōgon and…

emperor-go-kogon.s: Emperor Go-Kōgon was the fourth emperor of the Northern Court of Japan, reigning from 1352 to 1371. A son of Emperor Kōgon, he was enthroned by the Ashikaga after Southern forces carried off the senior members of the Northern imperial family, and he was crowned without the…

emperor-go-enyu.s: Emperor Go-En'yū was the fifth emperor of the Northern Court of Japan, reigning from 1371 to 1382. A son of Go-Kōgon, he reigned during the ascendancy of the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, who dominated the court.

emperor-go-komatsu.s: Emperor Go-Komatsu was the sixth and last emperor of the Northern Court of Japan and the 100th emperor in the traditional count, reigning from 1382 to 1412. In 1392 the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu arranged the return of the imperial regalia by the Southern emperor Go-Kameyama,…

erzhu-rong.s: Erzhu Rong was a frontier chieftain from northern Shanxi and a general of the Northern Wei dynasty. During the Six Garrisons rebellion he built a powerful army, and in 528, after the empress dowager Hu poisoned her son, he marched on Luoyang, enthroned Emperor Xiaozhuang and…

esen-taishi.s: Esen Taishi was a leader of the Oirat Mongols who dominated Mongolia in the mid-15th century, ruling through a puppet Genghisid khan. In 1449 he defeated a Ming army at Tumu and captured the Zhengtong Emperor.

edmund-ironside.s: Edmund Ironside was king of the English for seven months in 1016, the son of Æthelred the Unready. He resisted Cnut's invasion vigorously, earning his nickname, but was defeated at the Battle of Assandun in October 1016.

edward-the-confessor.s: Edward the Confessor was king of the English from 1042 to 1066, the son of Æthelred the Unready and Emma of Normandy. Raised in exile in Normandy during the Danish rule of Cnut and his sons, he succeeded his half-brother Harthacnut.

emma-of-normandy.s: Emma of Normandy was a daughter of Duke Richard I of Normandy who was twice queen of England, first as wife of Æthelred the Unready from 1002 and then of Cnut the Great from 1017. She was the mother of the kings Harthacnut and Edward the Confessor.

edmund-allenby.s: Edmund Allenby, 1st Viscount Allenby, was a British cavalry officer and field marshal. Commanding the Egyptian Expeditionary Force from 1917, he took Beersheba and Gaza and entered Jerusalem in December 1917, then routed the Ottoman armies at Megiddo in September 1918 and…

enryaku-ji.s: Enryaku-ji is a Buddhist monastery on Mount Hiei near Kyoto, founded by the monk Saichō in 788 and the head temple of the Tendai school. Over the following centuries it grew into a vast complex with its own armies of warrior monks, who often intervened in the politics of the…

emil-river.s: The Emil is a river of Central Asia that rises in the Tarbagatai region of north-western Xinjiang, China, and flows west into Lake Alakol in Kazakhstan. Its valley and the upper Irtysh were the pastures given by Genghis Khan to his son Ögedei.

efik.s: The Efik are a people of south-eastern Nigeria, living mainly around Calabar in Cross River State and speaking a language closely related to Ibibio. Settling on the Calabar River in the 17th century, they became middlemen in the Atlantic slave trade and later the palm-oil…

ekpe.s: Ekpe, the leopard society, is a graded men's society of the Efik and neighbouring peoples of the Cross River region of Nigeria and Cameroon. In 18th- and 19th-century Old Calabar it acted as a government, making laws, settling disputes and enforcing debts, including those owed…

edward-augustus-freeman.s: Edward Augustus Freeman was an English historian and Regius Professor of Modern History at Oxford from 1884. His best-known work is the History of the Norman Conquest of England, and in his History of Federal Government he made the Achaean League a model of a federal state.

ekasarana-dharma.s: Ekasarana Dharma is the Vaishnavite religious movement founded in Assam by Srimanta Sankardev in the late fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. It teaches devotion to Krishna as the one God, expressed through congregational prayer, recitation and song rather than sacrifice, and…

encamp.s: Encamp is one of the seven parishes of Andorra and the name of its main town, on the Valira d'Orient in the centre of the principality. The parish includes Pas de la Casa, a ski resort and the main border crossing with France, and the town is linked to the Grandvalira ski area…

escaldes-engordany.s: Escaldes-Engordany is the seventh and newest parish of Andorra, separated from Andorra la Vella in 1978, with which it forms one continuous town. Its name refers to the hot springs that made it a spa resort, today centred on the Caldea thermal complex, and it is a major…

ernesto-sabato.s: Ernesto Sabato was an Argentine writer and physicist, author of the novels The Tunnel (1948) and On Heroes and Tombs (1961). In 1983 President Raúl Alfonsín appointed him to chair the national commission on the disappeared, CONADEP, whose report Nunca Más documented the crimes…

eva-peron.s: Eva Perón, known as Evita, was an Argentine actress who married Juan Perón in 1945 and became the most powerful woman in Argentine politics as first lady. Through her foundation she ran a vast programme of social aid, and she championed the women's suffrage law of 1947 and the…

eleusinian-mysteries.s: The Eleusinian Mysteries were the secret initiation rites of Demeter and her daughter Persephone, or Kore, held each year at Eleusis in Attica under the supervision of Athens. Initiates walked in procession from Athens along the Sacred Way and were promised a better fate after…

ephialtes-athenian-statesman.s: Ephialtes was an Athenian democratic politician who in 462/461 BCE carried reforms that stripped the aristocratic Council of the Areopagus of most of its political and judicial powers, transferring them to the Council of Five Hundred, the Assembly and the popular courts. He…
