erechtheion.s: The Erechtheion is an Ionic temple on the Acropolis of Athens, built around 421–406 BCE and dedicated to Athena Polias, Poseidon and the legendary king Erechtheus. Its unusual plan on uneven ground housed the ancient olive-wood image of Athena, and its south porch is carried…

eurycleides.s: Eurycleides of Kephisia was an Athenian statesman who, with his brother Micion, led the city in the later third century BCE. In 229 BCE, after the death of Demetrius II of Macedon, they raised money to pay the Macedonian commander Diogenes to withdraw his garrisons from…

emperor-ferdinand-northern-railway.s: The Emperor Ferdinand Northern Railway was the first steam railway in the Austrian Empire, financed by Salomon Rothschild and opened in 1837 between Floridsdorf and Deutsch-Wagram near Vienna. It reached Brünn in 1839 and was extended to the coal fields of Moravia and Silesia…

ekathotsarot.s: Ekathotsarot was king of Ayutthaya from 1605 to about 1610, younger brother and successor of Naresuan, with whom he had fought in the wars against Burma. His reign was peaceful, and he encouraged foreign trade, opening relations with the Dutch East India Company and sending a…

ekkathat.s: Ekkathat was the last king of Ayutthaya, reigning from 1758 to 1767 after his younger brother Uthumphon gave up the throne. Weak and faction-ridden, his court could not resist the Konbaung armies of Burma, which besieged the capital from 1766 and sacked it in April 1767;…

elizabeth-castle.s: Elizabeth Castle is a fortress on a tidal islet in St Aubin's Bay off Saint Helier, Jersey. Begun in the 1590s, when artillery had made Mont Orgueil vulnerable, it was named after Elizabeth I by Sir Walter Raleigh, governor of the island from 1600.

english-civil-war.s: The English Civil War was a series of wars from 1642 to 1651 between the supporters of King Charles I and of Parliament, part of the wider Wars of the Three Kingdoms in England, Scotland and Ireland. Parliament's victory led to the trial and execution of Charles I in 1649, the…

ekdala.s: Ekdala was a fortress of the Bengal Sultanate near Pandua, in present-day Malda region of Bengal, protected by rivers and marshes. In 1353–1354 Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah held out there against Firuz Shah Tughluq of Delhi, and in 1359 his son Sikandar Shah did the same; both sieges…

eumelus-of-bosporus.s: Eumelus was king of the Bosporan Kingdom from about 309 to 304 BCE, a son of Paerisades I. In the civil war after his father's death he allied with the native king Aripharnes against his brothers Satyrus II and Prytanis and won the throne.

edwin-lutyens.s: Sir Edwin Lutyens was an English architect known for country houses, war memorials and the planning of New Delhi as the capital of British India. With Herbert Baker he designed the new imperial city, and his Viceroy's House, now Rashtrapati Bhavan, and India Gate combine…

elibaal.s: Elibaal was a king of Byblos around 900 BCE. He is known from a Phoenician inscription on a statue of the pharaoh Osorkon I, now in the Louvre, which he dedicated to the Baalat Gebal, the goddess of Byblos.

enylus.s: Enylus was the last known independent king of Byblos under Persian rule in the fourth century BCE, known from his coins and from the historian Arrian. In 332 BCE, learning that Byblos had already submitted to Alexander the Great, he left the Persian fleet and brought his ships…

ernest-renan.s: Ernest Renan was a French scholar of Semitic languages, historian of religion and essayist. In 1860–1861 he led a French archaeological mission to Lebanon that explored Byblos, Tyre and Sidon, published as Mission de Phénicie.

eucharist.s: The Eucharist, also called Holy Communion or the Lord's Supper, is the Christian rite of bread and wine commemorating the Last Supper of Jesus. Its meaning divided the Reformation: Catholics taught transubstantiation, Luther a real bodily presence, and Zwingli a symbolic…

eth-zurich.s: ETH Zurich is a public university of science and technology in Zürich, founded by the Swiss federal state as the Federal Polytechnic School and opened in 1855. It became one of the leading technical universities in the world; Albert Einstein studied and later taught there, and…

etemenanki.s: Etemenanki, 'temple of the foundation of heaven and earth', was the ziggurat of Marduk in Babylon, standing beside his temple Esagila. Rebuilt on a vast scale by Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar II, it rose in stepped stages over a base about 91 metres square.

emporio-chios.s: Emporio is a harbour site on the south coast of Chios in Greece, excavated by the British School at Athens in the 1950s. It revealed a long-lived Bronze Age settlement with links to the Minoan and Mycenaean worlds, and an Archaic hilltop town of the seventh and sixth centuries…

edmond-van-eetvelde.s: Edmond van Eetvelde was a Belgian official who served Leopold II as administrator-general of foreign affairs of the Congo Free State from 1885 and as its secretary of state from 1894. Working from Brussels, he was one of the chief architects of the state's administration and…

escaut-department.s: Escaut was a department of the French Republic and Empire, formed in 1795 when France annexed the Austrian Netherlands. Named after the French name of the Scheldt, it covered the eastern part of the former County of Flanders together with Zeelandic Flanders, and its capital…

early-netherlandish-painting.s: Early Netherlandish painting is the work of painters active in the Burgundian and Habsburg Netherlands in the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, often called the Flemish Primitives. Working mainly in Bruges, Ghent, Tournai and Brussels, artists such as Jan van Eyck,…

estates-of-hainaut.s: The Estates of Hainaut were the representative assembly of the County of Hainaut, made up of the clergy, the nobility and the towns. From the fourteenth century they met at Mons to vote the taxes and subsidies requested by the count and defended the county's charters and…

edvard-benes.s: Edvard Beneš was a Czech politician who worked with Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk for Czechoslovak independence and served as foreign minister from 1918 to 1935. As president from 1935, he resigned after the Munich Agreement of 1938, led the government in exile in London and returned…

enfield-london.s: Enfield is a town in north London, now the centre of a London borough. From 1816 to 1988 it was the site of the Royal Small Arms Factory at Enfield Lock, which made the Lee-Enfield rifle and the Bren light machine gun for the British armed forces.

eurocommunism.s: Eurocommunism was a trend among West European communist parties in the 1970s and 1980s, led by the Italian party under Enrico Berlinguer and the Spanish party under Santiago Carrillo. Eurocommunists claimed independence from the Soviet Union and accepted parliamentary…

ea-nasir.s: Ea-nasir was a merchant of Ur around 1750 BCE who imported copper by way of Dilmun. He is known from tablets found in his house, above all a letter in which a customer, Nanni, complains angrily about poor-quality copper and rude treatment.

edward-the-black-prince.s: Edward the Black Prince (Edward of Woodstock) was the eldest son of Edward III of England and a celebrated commander of the Hundred Years' War. He fought at Crécy in 1346, captured John II of France at Poitiers in 1356 and ruled Aquitaine as its prince from 1362.

everard-tserclaes.s: Everard t'Serclaes was a Brussels patrician and a hero of the War of the Brabantine Succession. In October 1356, after the Flemish had occupied Brussels following the Battle of Scheut, he led a small band that entered the city by night and drove out the Flemish garrison.

estates-of-brittany.s: The Estates of Brittany were the representative assembly of the Duchy of Brittany, bringing together clergy, nobles and towns from the fifteenth century to vote taxes and advise the duke. After the union with France, which they approved at Vannes in 1532, they defended the…

estates-of-burgundy.s: The Estates of Burgundy were the assembly of clergy, nobles and towns of the Duchy of Burgundy, meeting from the fourteenth century to vote taxes for the duke and later for the French king. After the duchy was annexed by Louis XI in 1477, they kept Burgundy's status as a pays…

emmanuel-here.s: Emmanuel Héré was an architect from Lorraine who served Stanisław Leszczyński, duke of Lorraine and Bar, at Nancy and Lunéville. He designed the Place Royale, now Place Stanislas, with its town hall, together with the adjoining Place de la Carrière and Place d'Alliance in…

exchequer-of-normandy.s: The Exchequer of Normandy was the financial and judicial court of the duchy of Normandy, sitting at Caen under the Anglo-Norman kings. Like the English Exchequer, it audited the accounts of local officials, and its earliest surviving roll dates from 1180.

eilhard-lubinus.s: Eilhard Lubinus was a German scholar and professor at the University of Rostock who taught poetry, mathematics and theology. Commissioned by Duke Philip II of Pomerania, he travelled through the duchy and produced the great map of Pomerania published in 1618, decorated with…

eike-von-repgow.s: Eike von Repgow was a Saxon knight and legal expert who compiled the Sachsenspiegel, the most important German law book of the Middle Ages, between about 1220 and 1235. He wrote it first in Latin and then in Middle Low German, recording the customary land law and feudal law of…

emperor-fei-of-jin.s: Emperor Fei of Jin, personal name Sima Yi, reigned over the Eastern Jin dynasty from 365 to 371. Real power lay with the general Huan Wen, who in 371 deposed him on the pretext that his sons were not his own and reduced him to the rank of Duke of Haixi.

east-semitic-languages.s: The East Semitic languages are an extinct branch of the Semitic language family, spoken in ancient Mesopotamia and Syria. They include Akkadian, with its Babylonian and Assyrian dialects, and probably Eblaite, the language of the archives of Ebla.

enna-dagan.s: Enna-Dagan was a king of Mari on the Euphrates in the twenty-fourth century BCE. He is known chiefly from a letter found in the archives of Ebla in which he recounts the campaigns of Mari's kings, among them Iblul-Il, against towns in Ebla's sphere of influence.

elizabeth-charlotte-madame-palatine.s: Elizabeth Charlotte of the Palatinate, known as Liselotte, was a daughter of Elector Charles I Louis who married Philippe, Duke of Orléans, brother of Louis XIV, in 1671. When her brother Charles II died without heirs in 1685, Louis XIV claimed Palatine lands in her name, a…

elizabeth-stuart-queen-of-bohemia.s: Elizabeth Stuart was the daughter of James VI and I and the wife of Frederick V, Elector Palatine, whom she married in 1613. Her husband's acceptance of the Bohemian crown made her queen for a single winter in 1619–1620, hence her name, the Winter Queen, and the couple spent…

ezzonids.s: The Ezzonids were a noble dynasty of Lotharingia, named after Ezzo, count palatine of Lotharingia (died 1034), who married Matilda, daughter of Emperor Otto II. They held the palatine office in Lotharingia in the eleventh century, with lands around Aachen, Bonn and Cologne,…

ehrenfried-walther-von-tschirnhaus.s: Ehrenfried Walther von Tschirnhaus was a Saxon mathematician, physicist and philosopher who corresponded with Leibniz and Spinoza. He built large burning mirrors and lenses to study the melting of materials at high temperatures, and in Dresden he worked with Johann Friedrich…

eulogius-of-cordoba.s: Eulogius of Córdoba was a Christian priest and writer in Umayyad al-Andalus and the chief chronicler and defender of the Martyrs of Córdoba. His Memoriale sanctorum records Christians executed in the 850s for denouncing Islam or for apostasy.

eugenios-of-trebizond.s: Saint Eugenios was an early Christian martyr of Trebizond, said to have been executed under Diocletian around 300, and the patron saint of the city. His church was its main shrine, and the emperors of Trebizond struck silver aspers bearing his image.

erkesiya.s: The Erkesiya is a long earthwork rampart with a ditch in Thrace, in south-eastern Bulgaria, running inland from the Black Sea coast near Develtos. It roughly follows the frontier fixed between Bulgaria and Byzantium by the peace of 815/816 and served to mark and defend the…

eugenius.s: Eugenius (died 394) was western Roman emperor from 392 to 394, a teacher of rhetoric raised to the throne by the Frankish general Arbogast after the death of Valentinian II. Though a Christian, he tolerated a revival of paganism among the Roman senatorial aristocracy.

ecole-francaise-dextreme-orient.s: The École française d'Extrême-Orient is a French institute for the study of Asian civilisations, established in 1900 with its headquarters in Hanoi and since the 1950s in Paris. Its scholars studied the languages, religions and archaeology of Indochina and beyond, and it…

elysee-accords.s: The Élysée Accords were agreements signed on 8 March 1949 by the French President Vincent Auriol and the former emperor Bảo Đại. They recognised Vietnam, including Cochinchina, as an Associated State within the French Union under Bảo Đại, while France kept control of defence…

erfurt-union.s: The Erfurt Union was a Prussian attempt in 1849–1850 to unite the German states, excluding Austria, in a federation under Prussian leadership after King Frederick William IV refused the imperial crown offered by the Frankfurt Parliament. A union parliament met in Erfurt in…

eulji-mundeok.s: Eulji Mundeok was a Goguryeo general who led the defence against the invasion of Emperor Yang of Sui in 612. He drew a large Sui force deep into Goguryeo territory, feigning retreat, and then destroyed it at the Salsu River during its withdrawal, inflicting one of the heaviest…

electorate-of-cologne.s: The Electorate of Cologne was the ecclesiastical principality of the archbishops of Cologne within the Holy Roman Empire, one of its seven original electorates. Besides lands along the Rhine, governed from Bonn after the city of Cologne won its freedom, the archbishops ruled…

emanuel-merck.s: Emanuel Merck was a German pharmacist who turned his family's pharmacy in Darmstadt into an industrial firm. From 1827 he began manufacturing alkaloids such as morphine on a large scale for doctors and pharmacists.

esch-sur-alzette.s: Esch-sur-Alzette is the second-largest city of Luxembourg, in the south of the country near the French border. It grew from a small town into the centre of the Luxembourg steel industry after the iron ore of the region, the minette, was exploited from the late nineteenth century.

eurobond.s: A Eurobond is an international bond issued in a currency other than that of the country where it is sold, usually underwritten by an international syndicate of banks. The modern Eurobond market began in 1963 with a dollar loan for the Italian motorway company Autostrade,…

european-commission.s: The European Commission is the executive body of the European Union, which proposes legislation, enforces the treaties and manages common policies. It grew from the High Authority of the European Coal and Steel Community and the commissions of the European Economic Community…

european-court-of-auditors.s: The European Court of Auditors is the institution that audits the finances of the European Union. Created by a treaty of 1975, it began work in 1977 and is based in Luxembourg.

elena-glinskaya.s: Elena Glinskaya was the second wife of Vasily III of Moscow and the mother of Ivan IV, for whom she ruled as regent from 1533 until her death in 1538. Of a Lithuanian princely family that had fled to Moscow, she imprisoned rival claimants, including her husband's brothers, and…

euridice-peri.s: Euridice is an opera by Jacopo Peri to a libretto by Ottavio Rinuccini, first performed on 6 October 1600 at the Pitti Palace in Florence during the celebrations for the wedding of Maria de' Medici and Henry IV of France. Based on the myth of Orpheus and Eurydice, it is the…

eighth-crusade.s: The Eighth Crusade was the expedition led by Louis IX of France against Tunis in 1270. The crusaders landed at Carthage in July, hoping to convert or subdue the Hafsid ruler al-Mustansir, but disease swept the camp and Louis died there in August.

emperor-jing-of-han.s: Emperor Jing of Han, born Liu Qi, was the sixth emperor of the Western Han dynasty, ruling from 157 to 141 BCE. Early in his reign he suppressed the Rebellion of the Seven States of 154 BCE and then cut back the powers of the semi-autonomous kingdoms.

euric.s: Euric was king of the Visigoths from 466 to 484, having taken the throne by murdering his brother Theodoric II. Breaking with Rome, he extended Visigothic rule over most of Gaul south of the Loire and, in the 470s, over Hispania Tarraconensis, ending Roman rule in Iberia.

ereyanga.s: Ereyanga was a Hoysala prince of the late 11th century, the son of Vinayaditya, who served as a leading commander of the Western Chalukya king Vikramaditya VI. His service raised the standing of the Hoysala family.

east-kalimantan.s: East Kalimantan is a province of Indonesia on the eastern side of the island of Borneo, with its capital at Samarinda and the oil city of Balikpapan. Its rivers were home to the early Hindu kingdom of Kutai, whose Sanskrit inscriptions are among the oldest in Indonesia.

emilio-de-bono.s: Emilio De Bono was an Italian general and one of the four leaders of Mussolini's March on Rome in 1922. He served as governor of Tripolitania and minister of the colonies, and in October 1935 commanded the invasion of Ethiopia until Pietro Badoglio replaced him in November.

emperor-taizong-of-jin.s: Emperor Taizong of Jin, Wanyan Wuqimai, was the second emperor of the Jurchen Jin dynasty, ruling from 1123 to 1135 after his brother Aguda. In 1125 his armies captured the last Liao emperor, Tianzuo, ending the Liao state.

emperor-zhangzong-of-jin.s: Emperor Zhangzong of Jin, Wanyan Jing, ruled the Jurchen Jin dynasty from 1189 to 1208. A grandson of Shizong, he was a calligrapher and patron of Chinese learning, and his reign marked the height of Confucian government, with the Taihe Code of 1201.

esim-khan.s: Esim Khan was khan of the Kazakhs from 1598 to 1628, succeeding his brother Tauekel Khan. He kept most of the Syr Darya towns his brother had taken from the Bukharan Shaybanids, with Turkistan as his main seat, and fought a long contest with his rival Tursun Khan of Tashkent,…

elipandus.s: Elipandus was archbishop of Toledo in the late eighth century, when the city was under Muslim rule. He was the leading advocate of Adoptionism, the teaching that Christ in his humanity was the adopted Son of God, which he defended in letters against Beatus of Liébana and the…

ermesinda.s: Ermesinda was a daughter of Pelagius, founder of the Kingdom of Asturias. Her marriage to Alfonso, son of Duke Peter of Cantabria, joined Asturias and Cantabria, and on the death of her brother Favila in 739 the throne passed to her husband as Alfonso I.

expo-58.s: Expo 58 was the world's fair held in Brussels from April to October 1958, the first major international exposition after the Second World War. Its theme was a more humane world built on scientific progress, and it drew more than 40 million visits.

eupen.s: Eupen is a town in the province of Liège in eastern Belgium, near the German border. Part of Prussia from 1815, it was transferred with Malmedy to Belgium under the Treaty of Versailles after the First World War, annexed by Germany in 1940 and returned in 1944.

eleanor-of-england-queen-of-castile.n: Eleanor of England, Queen of Castile
eleanor-of-england-queen-of-castile.s: Eleanor of England was a daughter of Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine who married Alfonso VIII of Castile in 1177. She was a patron of religious houses, including the royal convent of Las Huelgas at Burgos, and of troubadours.

eamont-bridge.s: Eamont Bridge is a village in Cumbria, England, just south of Penrith on the River Eamont. On 12 July 927 the English king Æthelstan received there the submission of Constantine II of Scotland, Owain of Strathclyde and other northern rulers, according to the Anglo-Saxon…

edgar-king-of-england.s: Edgar, known as the Peaceful, was king of the English from 959 to 975. His reign was free of major invasion, and he supported the Benedictine monastic reform led by Dunstan, Æthelwold and Oswald.

encyclopedie.s: The Encyclopédie was a French encyclopaedia edited by Denis Diderot and, until 1759, Jean le Rond d'Alembert, published in 17 volumes of text and 11 of plates between 1751 and 1772. With contributions from Voltaire, Montesquieu, Rousseau and many others, it aimed to gather all…

eastern-thrace.s: Eastern Thrace is the European part of Turkey, between the Maritsa river and the Bosporus, including Istanbul and Edirne. The Treaty of Sèvres assigned most of it to Greece in 1920, but after Greek defeat in Anatolia the Armistice of Mudanya in 1922 and the Treaty of Lausanne…

ednyfed-fychan.s: Ednyfed Fychan was the steward, or distain, of Gwynedd under Llywelyn the Great and his son Dafydd ap Llywelyn, from about 1215 until his death in 1246. He led the princes' administration and diplomacy and was rewarded with lands held free of most dues.

edward-i-of-england.s: Edward I was king of England from 1272 to 1307. He conquered the principality of Gwynedd in the wars of 1277 and 1282–1283, after which he secured north Wales with castles such as Caernarfon, Conwy and Harlech, and he later fought long wars to subdue Scotland.

edmund-burke.s: Edmund Burke was an Irish-born statesman, orator and political thinker, educated at Trinity College Dublin. As a Whig member of the British Parliament he supported conciliation with the American colonies and relief for Irish Catholics, and he led the impeachment of Warren…

edward-lovett-pearce.s: Sir Edward Lovett Pearce was an Irish architect and the leading figure of Palladian architecture in Ireland. His major work, the Parliament House on College Green in Dublin, begun in 1729, was the first purpose-built two-chamber parliament building in the world.

earl-of-kildare.s: Earl of Kildare is a title in the peerage of Ireland created in 1316 for John FitzGerald and held by the Geraldine (FitzGerald) family. In the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries the earls, above all Gerald FitzGerald, 'the Great Earl', governed Ireland as lord…

elisha.s: Elisha was a prophet of the northern Kingdom of Israel in the ninth century BCE, the disciple and successor of Elijah according to the Books of Kings. The stories about him include miracles of healing and provision as well as a political role: he is said to have foretold…

enrico-fermi.s: Enrico Fermi was an Italian physicist who built the first nuclear reactor. Working in Rome, he showed that slow neutrons could induce radioactivity and received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1938.

expedition-of-the-thousand.s: The Expedition of the Thousand was the campaign led by Giuseppe Garibaldi in 1860, in which about a thousand volunteers in red shirts sailed from near Genoa and landed at Marsala in Sicily in May. They defeated the Bourbon forces, took Palermo and crossed to the mainland,…

earl-of-mercia.s: The Earl of Mercia was one of the great territorial earls of late Anglo-Saxon England, governing much of the old Mercian kingdom under the kings of England. Under Cnut and Edward the Confessor the earldom was held by Leofric and then by his son Ælfgar and grandson Edwin.

eyre-coote.s: Sir Eyre Coote was an Irish-born British army officer who served in India. He commanded the East India Company's forces at the Battle of Wandiwash in 1760, which broke French power in southern India, and returned as commander-in-chief in India in 1779.

eadberht-of-northumbria.s: Eadberht (died 768) was king of Northumbria from 737 to 758, ruling in partnership with his brother Ecgbert, archbishop of York. He issued coins in his own name, annexed Kyle in Ayrshire in 750 and in 756, with the Pictish king Óengus, forced the Britons of Dumbarton to…

eadred.s: Eadred (c. 923–955) was king of the English from 946 to 955, a son of Edward the Elder and younger brother of Æthelstan and Edmund.

ealdred-of-bamburgh.s: Ealdred was the ruler of Bamburgh and the northern part of the former Northumbrian kingdom in the early tenth century, son of Eadwulf. Driven out for a time by the Norse king Ragnall, he submitted to Edward the Elder in 920 and to Æthelstan at Eamont in 927, when the northern…

eboracum.s: Eboracum was the Roman fortress and city on the site of York, founded around 71 AD as the base of the Ninth Legion. It became the capital of the province of Britannia Inferior; the emperor Septimius Severus died there in 211, and Constantine the Great was proclaimed emperor…

ecgbert-of-york.s: Ecgbert (died 766) was bishop of York from 732 and, from 735, the first archbishop of York since Paulinus, after obtaining the pallium from Rome. A brother of King Eadberht of Northumbria, he ruled the church while his brother ruled the kingdom.

edvard-grieg.s: Edvard Grieg (1843–1907) was a Norwegian composer and pianist from Bergen, the leading figure of Norwegian Romantic music. Drawing on folk melodies, he wrote the Piano Concerto in A minor, the incidental music to Ibsen's Peer Gynt, including "In the Hall of the Mountain King",…

edvard-munch.s: Edvard Munch (1863–1944) was a Norwegian painter and printmaker and a pioneer of Expressionism. His work dealt with anxiety, love, illness and death, themes drawn from a childhood marked by loss.

ekofisk.s: Ekofisk is an oil field in the Norwegian sector of the North Sea, discovered by Phillips Petroleum in 1969 and in production from 1971. The first major petroleum find on the Norwegian continental shelf, it opened the way to an oil and gas industry that transformed Norway into…

edward-lhuyd.s: Edward Lhuyd was a Welsh naturalist, antiquary and linguist, keeper of the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford from 1690. He travelled through Wales and the other Celtic countries recording inscriptions, fossils and plants, and in 1696 copied the inscription of the Pillar of Eliseg.

eratosthenes.s: Eratosthenes of Cyrene was a Greek scholar who became head of the Library of Alexandria under the Ptolemies. He made a remarkably close estimate of the Earth's circumference from the angle of the sun at Syene and Alexandria, drew a map of the known world with lines of latitude…

edward-balliol.s: Edward Balliol was the son of King John Balliol and a claimant to the Scottish throne. In 1332, backed by the English 'Disinherited' nobles, he invaded Scotland, won the Battle of Dupplin Moor and was crowned at Scone, opening the Second War of Scottish Independence.

edict-of-paris.s: The Edict of Paris was issued by the Frankish king Chlothar II on 18 October 614, soon after he had reunited the Frankish kingdoms, following a church council in Paris. It confirmed the rights of the church and the aristocracy and required royal officials to be appointed from…

eanfrith-of-bernicia.s: Eanfrith was king of Bernicia, the northern part of Northumbria, in 633–634, the eldest son of King Æthelfrith. During the reign of Edwin he lived in exile among the Picts, where he fathered Talorgan, later king of the Picts from 653 to 657.

ecgfrith-of-northumbria.s: Ecgfrith was king of Northumbria from 670 to 685, the son of Oswiu. He extended Northumbrian rule over the southern Picts and founded a bishopric at Abercorn on the Forth, but lost Lindsey to Æthelred of Mercia after the Battle of the Trent in 679.

ecgfrith-of-mercia.s: Ecgfrith was king of Mercia for a few months in 796, the only son of Offa. In 787 Offa had him consecrated as king during his own lifetime, the first recorded royal anointing in England, to secure the succession.

ecclesiastical-history-of-the-english-pe.s: The Ecclesiastical History of the English People is a Latin history of the English church and peoples completed by Bede at Jarrow in 731. eduard-morike.s: Eduard Mörike was a German poet and Lutheran pastor from Ludwigsburg in Württemberg, associated with the Swabian school of poets. His lyric poems, many set to music by Hugo Wolf, and his novella Mozart on the Way to Prague (1855) made him one of the finest German writers of…

el-kurru.s: El-Kurru is a royal cemetery near Napata in northern Sudan, burial place of the early kings of Kush. The tombs of Kashta, Piye, Shabaka, Shebitku and Tantamani lie there, with pyramids built in the Egyptian manner, and the kings' horses were buried nearby.

emperor-daozong-of-liao.s: Emperor Daozong of Liao, born Yelü Hongji, reigned from 1055 to 1101. A devout Buddhist, he sponsored lavish religious foundations and the printing of the Liao Buddhist canon, but his reign was troubled by court factions: the empress was forced to commit suicide in 1075 and…

emperor-muzong-of-liao.s: Emperor Muzong of Liao, born Yelü Jing, reigned from 951 to 969. Remembered for his heavy drinking and long sleeps, he neglected government and ruled harshly over his attendants, by whom he was murdered in 969.

emperor-shizong-of-liao.s: Emperor Shizong of Liao, born Yelü Ruan, was a grandson of the founder Abaoji who seized the throne in 947 on the death of Taizong, defeating the supporters of the Empress Dowager Shulü Ping. He extended Chinese-style administration but was murdered in a court conspiracy in…

emperor-xingzong-of-liao.s: Emperor Xingzong of Liao, born Yelü Zongzhen, reigned from 1031 to 1055. ecomog.s: ECOMOG, the Economic Community of West African States Monitoring Group, was a multinational West African armed force led by Nigeria. Formed in 1990 to intervene in the Liberian civil war, it held Monrovia and later supervised the 1997 elections; it also intervened in Sierra…

edward-james-roye.s: Edward James Roye was the fifth president of Liberia, serving from 1870 to 1871. Born in Ohio, he became a wealthy merchant and the first president of full African descent.

edward-wilmot-blyden.s: Edward Wilmot Blyden was a writer, educator and statesman born in the Danish West Indies who emigrated to Liberia in 1850. evora.s: Évora is a city in the Alentejo region of southern Portugal. As Roman Ebora Liberalitas Julia it was a municipality of Lusitania, and its well-preserved Roman temple of the 1st century CE is among the best-known Roman monuments in Portugal.

eumenes-of-cardia.s: Eumenes of Cardia was a Greek general and scholar from Cardia in the Thracian Chersonese who served as royal secretary to Philip II and Alexander the Great. After Alexander's death in 323 BCE he received Cappadocia and Paphlagonia and fought for the Argead royal house in the…

edict-of-potsdam.s: The Edict of Potsdam was issued by Frederick William, the Great Elector of Brandenburg, in October 1685 in response to Louis XIV's revocation of the Edict of Nantes. It offered French Huguenot refugees safe settlement, tax exemptions and freedom of worship, and some 20,000…

expulsion-of-the-salzburg-protestants.s: The expulsion of the Salzburg Protestants was the forced emigration of some 20,000 Lutherans from the Archbishopric of Salzburg, ordered by Archbishop Leopold Anton von Firmian in his edict of 1731. Most were welcomed by King Frederick William I of Prussia, who settled them in…

el-lahun.s: El-Lahun is an archaeological site at the entrance to the Faiyum in Egypt, where Senusret II built his pyramid. Nearby lay Kahun, the planned town for the officials and workers of his pyramid cult, excavated by Flinders Petrie in 1889.

einsatzgruppen.s: The Einsatzgruppen were mobile killing units of the SS and police that followed the German armies into Poland in 1939 and into the Soviet Union in 1941. Behind the front they shot Jews, communist officials, Roma and others in mass executions, such as at Babi Yar near Kyiv,…

ernst-rohm.s: Ernst Röhm was a German officer and early Nazi leader who commanded the SA, the party's paramilitary stormtroopers, which grew to millions of members by 1933. His demands for a 'second revolution' and for the SA to absorb the army alarmed the generals and Hitler's conservative…

edward-braddock.s: Edward Braddock was a British general sent to North America in 1755 as commander-in-chief at the start of the French and Indian War. Leading an expedition against Fort Duquesne, he was defeated and mortally wounded by French and Native forces at the Battle of the Monongahela…

edmund-hillary.s: Edmund Hillary was a New Zealand mountaineer and explorer who, with the Sherpa Tenzing Norgay, made the first confirmed ascent of Mount Everest on 29 May 1953. He later reached the South Pole overland in 1958 during the Commonwealth Trans-Antarctic Expedition.

euthymius-ii-of-novgorod.s: Euthymius II was Archbishop of Novgorod from 1429 to 1458 and one of the most powerful figures of the late Novgorod Republic. ercole-consalvi.s: Ercole Consalvi was an Italian cardinal and cardinal secretary of state to Pope Pius VII. He negotiated the Concordat of 1801 with Napoleon and, at the Congress of Vienna in 1815, recovered almost all the Papal States for the pope.

ernest-of-bavaria.s: Ernest of Bavaria was a Wittelsbach prince and churchman who became prince-bishop of Liège in 1581 and archbishop-elector of Cologne in 1583, along with several other sees. His election began over a century of Bavarian rule in Liège, and his victory in the Cologne War secured…

european-free-trade-association.s: The European Free Trade Association is a free-trade organisation founded in 1960 by seven European states outside the European Economic Community. eastern-carpathians.s: The Eastern Carpathians are the section of the Carpathian mountains running through south-eastern Poland, Slovakia, Ukraine and northern Romania. They formed the western boundary of medieval Moldavia, separating it from Transylvania.

eastern-chalukyas.s: The Eastern Chalukyas were a dynasty that ruled the Vengi region of coastal Andhra, between the Godavari and Krishna rivers, from 624 to about 1070. Founded by Kubja Vishnuvardhana, a brother of the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II, they long fought the Rashtrakutas.

edward-pellew-1st-viscount-exmouth.s: Edward Pellew, 1st Viscount Exmouth, was a British naval officer celebrated as a frigate captain in the wars with Revolutionary France. As commander in the Mediterranean, he led an Anglo-Dutch fleet that bombarded Algiers on 27 August 1816, destroying much of the corsair fleet…

el-alto.s: El Alto is a city on the Altiplano of Bolivia, on the plateau rim above La Paz, at an altitude of about 4,150 metres. Once a suburb, it grew rapidly from migrants from the countryside and former miners, became a separate municipality in 1985, and is now one of the largest…

eduardo-frei-montalva.s: Eduardo Frei Montalva was a founder of Chile's Christian Democratic Party and president from 1964 to 1970. His 'Revolution in Liberty' expanded land reform, organised peasant unions and acquired a majority stake for the state in the large copper mines.

el-teniente.s: El Teniente is the largest underground copper mine in the world, in the Andes near Rancagua in central Chile. It was developed from 1905 by the Braden Copper Company, later owned by Kennecott, and supported the mining town of Sewell.

emil-korner.s: Emil Körner was a Prussian army officer hired by Chile in 1885 to modernise its army. He reformed military education and organisation on German lines, and during the civil war of 1891 he sided with Congress and helped plan its victory over President Balmaceda.

eloy-alfaro.s: Eloy Alfaro was the leader of Ecuador's Liberal Revolution of 1895 and president from 1895 to 1901 and from 1906 to 1911. He separated church and state, introduced civil marriage and secular education, and completed the Guayaquil–Quito railway in 1908.

edwin-kemmerer.s: Edwin Kemmerer was an American economist at Princeton University known as the 'money doctor'. In the 1920s he led financial missions to Colombia, Chile, Ecuador, Bolivia, Peru, Poland and other countries, recommending central banks, the gold standard and budget reforms.

el-oro-province.s: El Oro is a coastal province in southern Ecuador on the border with Peru, with its capital at Machala. It is a major producer of bananas and shrimp and has gold mines in its uplands, which give it its name.

escuela-politecnica-nacional.s: The Escuela Politécnica Nacional is a public university of engineering and science in Quito, founded in 1869 by President Gabriel García Moreno. He brought German Jesuit scientists to teach there, making it a centre of scientific study in Ecuador.

el-mozote-massacre.s: The El Mozote massacre was the killing of more than 800 civilians, many of them children, by the Atlacatl Battalion of the Salvadoran army in and around the village of El Mozote, in Morazán department, on 11–12 December 1981. It was the largest massacre of the Salvadoran civil…

estonian-cultural-autonomy-act.s: The Estonian Cultural Autonomy Act of February 1925 allowed national minorities of at least 3,000 people to form self-governing bodies to run their own schools and cultural institutions, financed partly by taxing their members. It was used by the German and Jewish communities…

estonian-defence-league.s: The Estonian Defence League, or Kaitseliit, is a voluntary armed national defence organisation founded in November 1918 during the War of Independence. It grew into a large militia in the interwar republic and was dissolved after the Soviet occupation in 1940.

era-of-silence.s: The Era of Silence was the period of authoritarian rule in Estonia that began with Konstantin Päts's self-coup of 12 March 1934, carried out with General Johan Laidoner to prevent the Vaps movement from winning power. Parliament was suspended, parties were banned and the press…

estonian-declaration-of-independence.s: The Estonian Declaration of Independence, formally the Manifesto to the Peoples of Estonia, was issued by the Salvation Committee and proclaimed in Pärnu on 23 February and in Tallinn on 24 February 1918, between the Bolshevik withdrawal and the German occupation. It declared…

efrain-rios-montt.s: Efraín Ríos Montt (1926–2018) was a Guatemalan general who ruled as head of state after a coup from March 1982 to August 1983. His counter-insurgency campaign in the highlands, with scorched-earth tactics and forced civil patrols, killed thousands of Maya villagers.

el-senor-presidente.s: El Señor Presidente is a novel by the Guatemalan writer Miguel Ángel Asturias, written largely in the 1920s and 1930s and published in 1946. Portraying an unnamed Latin American country under a cruel and all-powerful dictator, modelled on Manuel Estrada Cabrera, it uses…

escuela-politecnica-guatemala.s: The Escuela Politécnica is the military academy of Guatemala, founded in 1873 by the liberal president Justo Rufino Barrios to train professional officers for a modern army. Its graduates formed the core of the officer corps that dominated Guatemalan politics for much of the…

esquipulas-peace-agreement.s: The Esquipulas Peace Agreement, or Esquipulas II, was signed on 7 August 1987 in Guatemala City by the presidents of Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica, following a first summit at Esquipulas in Guatemala in 1986. Based on a plan by the Costa Rican…

election-commission-of-india.s: The Election Commission of India is the constitutional body that has organised elections to the national parliament, the state legislatures and the presidency since 1950. It ran the first general election of 1951–1952, with about 173 million voters, and has since conducted the…

ernesto-cardenal.s: Ernesto Cardenal was a Nicaraguan poet and Catholic priest, a leading figure of liberation theology in Latin America. He founded a Christian community on the Solentiname islands in Lake Nicaragua and supported the Sandinista revolution, serving as minister of culture from 1979…

el-chorrillo.s: El Chorrillo is a densely populated working-class district of Panama City, next to the old city and the former Canal Zone. It housed the headquarters of the Panama Defence Forces, the Comandancia, and was heavily damaged when American forces attacked it during the invasion of…

ernesto-perez-balladares.s: Ernesto Pérez Balladares is a Panamanian politician of the Democratic Revolutionary Party who was president of Panama from 1994 to 1999. erigavo.s: Erigavo (Ceerigaabo) is a town in northern Somalia, the capital of the Sanaag region, lying in the highlands near the Cal Madow mountains. It is claimed by Somaliland, which administers it, and by Puntland.

eskom.s: Eskom is South Africa's state-owned electricity utility, founded in 1923 as the Electricity Supply Commission. It generates most of the country's power, largely from coal, and built one of the largest utilities in the world.

exarchate-of-ravenna.s: The Exarchate of Ravenna was the Byzantine administration of Italy, headed by an exarch with civil and military authority, created in the late sixth century to defend the remaining imperial territories against the Lombards. Its lands included Ravenna, Rome, Naples and the…

eric-iv-of-denmark.s: Eric IV, known as Eric Ploughpenny after a tax he levied on ploughs, was king of Denmark from 1241 to 1250. His reign was dominated by conflict with his brothers and the Church.

ermine-street.s: Ermine Street was a major Roman road in Britain running north from London through Lincoln to York, built in the early years after the conquest of 43 CE. It carried troops and supplies to the northern frontier and remained a main route for centuries; much of its line is…

emperor-mingyuan-of-northern-wei.s: Emperor Mingyuan, personal name Tuoba Si, was the second emperor of the Northern Wei, reigning from 409 to 423. He came to the throne after his father Tuoba Gui was murdered, consolidated the state and late in his reign campaigned against the Liu Song in the south.

european-russia.s: European Russia is the western part of Russia, lying in Europe west of the Ural Mountains and the Ural River. Although it covers only about a quarter of the country's territory, it holds the great majority of the population, the capital Moscow and the main historic and…

eupalinos.s: Eupalinos of Megara was a Greek engineer of the sixth century BCE who built the aqueduct tunnel on Samos for the tyrant Polycrates. He had the tunnel dug from both ends through Mount Kastro, and the two teams met almost exactly in the middle, a feat of surveying admired by…

eresburg.s: The Eresburg was a Saxon hill fort on the site of modern Obermarsberg in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, above the Diemel valley. Charlemagne captured it in 772 at the start of the Saxon Wars and destroyed the nearby Irminsul, the Saxons' sacred pillar.

euthymius-of-tarnovo.s: Euthymius of Tarnovo was the last patriarch of medieval Bulgaria, from 1375 until the Ottoman capture of Tarnovo in 1393. A Hesychast monk and pupil of Theodosius of Tarnovo, he reformed the language and spelling of Church Slavonic books and wrote lives of saints.

erligang-culture.s: The Erligang culture is a Bronze Age culture of China dated to about 1600–1400 BCE, named after a site at Zhengzhou in Henan. Its centre was the large walled city at Zhengzhou, and its bronze vessels, cast in a uniform style, spread as far as Panlongcheng on the Yangtze.

emperor-bing-of-song.s: Emperor Bing of Song, personal name Zhao Bing, was the last emperor of the Song dynasty, enthroned as a child in 1278 by loyalists fleeing the Mongols along the southern coast. emperor-zhenzong-of-song.s: Emperor Zhenzong of Song was the third emperor of the Northern Song dynasty, reigning from 997 to 1022. After the Liao invasion of 1004 he concluded the Treaty of Chanyuan (1005), which bought lasting peace with annual payments of silk and silver.

eurypontid-dynasty.s: The Eurypontids were the junior of Sparta's two royal houses, reigning alongside the Agiads. They took their name from Eurypon, said to be a grandson of Procles, twin brother of the Agiad founder Eurysthenes, and claimed descent from Heracles.

emily-ruete.s: Emily Ruete, born Sayyida Salme, was a daughter of Said bin Sultan, ruler of Oman and Zanzibar. In 1866 she eloped with the German merchant Rudolph Heinrich Ruete, converted to Christianity and settled in Hamburg.

edward-whymper.s: Edward Whymper was an English mountaineer, engraver and author. On 14 July 1865 he led the first ascent of the Matterhorn, but four of his party were killed on the descent when a rope broke, a disaster that made the climb famous.

escher-wyss.s: Escher Wyss was a Swiss engineering company founded in Zurich in 1805 by Hans Caspar Escher and Salomon von Wyss, first as a cotton-spinning mill. It became one of the leading Swiss machine builders of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, producing water turbines, paddle…

edo-castle.s: Edo Castle was a flatland castle in Edo, modern Tokyo, first built by Ōta Dōkan in 1457. Tokugawa Ieyasu made it his seat in 1590, and it was rebuilt on a vast scale as the residence of the Tokugawa shoguns from 1603 to 1867, surrounded by moats and the mansions of the daimyo.

In 159 he used the palace eunuchs to destroy the powerful consort clan of Liang Ji, after which eunuchs dominated the court, and in 166 he began the Partisan Prohibitions against scholar-officials who…

elymians.s: The Elymians were an ancient people of north-western Sicily whose main towns were Segesta, Eryx and Entella. Greek writers such as Thucydides said they descended from Trojan refugees, and their language, known from short inscriptions, is still poorly understood.

egidian-constitutions.s: The Egidian Constitutions were a legal code for the Papal States issued in 1357 by Cardinal Gil Álvarez Carrillo de Albornoz, papal legate in Italy during the Avignon papacy. Named after his Latin name, Aegidius, they organised the provinces of the Church's state, the powers…

eleonora-fonseca-pimentel.s: Eleonora Fonseca Pimentel was a Neapolitan poet and journalist, born in Rome to a Portuguese noble family, who became a leading figure of the Parthenopean Republic of 1799. Once a member of the royal court, she turned to republicanism and edited the republic's official…

eudemus-general.s: Eudemus was a Macedonian officer whom Alexander the Great left in the Punjab after his campaign in India. After Alexander's death he took control of the region and murdered the Indian king Porus around 317 BCE.

eritrean-peoples-liberation-front.s: The Eritrean People's Liberation Front was the armed movement that won Eritrea's independence from Ethiopia. Formed in the early 1970s by groups that broke away from the Eritrean Liberation Front, it built a disciplined guerrilla army based in the mountains around Nakfa.

east-aceh-regency.s: East Aceh is a regency on the north-east coast of Aceh province, at the northern tip of Sumatra, Indonesia. It includes the area of Perlak, where Indonesian tradition places the earliest Muslim sultanate in the archipelago.

enipeus-thessaly.s: The Enipeus is a river of Thessaly in central Greece, which rises in the Othrys mountains and flows north past Pharsalus through the Thessalian plain to join the Peneus system. In Greek myth it was a river god loved by Tyro.

etruscans.s: The Etruscans were the people of ancient Etruria, in what is now Tuscany, western Umbria and northern Lazio in Italy, whose civilisation flourished from about 900 BCE. They spoke a non-Indo-European language written in an alphabet adapted from the Greek, lived in independent…

elateia.s: Elateia was the largest city of ancient Phocis in central Greece, in the Cephissus valley, commanding the route from Thessaly into Boeotia. Its sudden occupation by Philip II of Macedon in 339 BCE caused panic in Athens, famously described by Demosthenes, and led to the Battle…

eleutheria-plataea.s: The Eleutheria was a festival of freedom held at Plataea in Boeotia in honour of Zeus Eleutherios, commemorating the Greek victory over the Persians there in 479 BCE. Celebrated every four years with games, including a race in armour, it was accompanied by yearly rites at the…

elblag.s: Elbląg is a city in northern Poland near the Vistula Lagoon. Founded as Elbing in 1237 by the Teutonic Order and settlers from Lübeck, it received Lübeck law and became a leading Hanseatic port.

evripidis-bakirtzis.s: Evripidis Bakirtzis was a Greek army officer known as the 'Red Colonel' for his left-wing views. A veteran of the Balkan and Asia Minor wars, he joined the resistance during the Axis occupation and in March 1944 became the first president of the Political Committee of National…

evrytania.s: Evrytania is a mountainous regional unit of central Greece in the southern Pindus range, with its capital at Karpenisi. Remote and thinly populated, it was a stronghold of the Greek resistance during the Axis occupation, and in March 1944 EAM established the Political…

elba.s: Elba is the largest island of the Tuscan Archipelago, off the coast of Tuscany, Italy, facing Piombino. Its iron ore was mined from Etruscan times, when it was smelted at Populonia, until the 20th century.

el-jadida.s: El Jadida, formerly Mazagan, is a port city on the Atlantic coast of Morocco, south-west of Casablanca. The Portuguese fortified it from 1514 and made it their last stronghold in Morocco, holding it until 1769, when they evacuated it under siege.

edeirnion.s: Edeirnion was a medieval commote in north-east Wales, in the upper Dee valley around Corwen. Part of the Kingdom of Powys and later of Powys Fadog, it was included after the English conquest in the county of Merioneth and is now in Denbighshire.

eteocretans.s: The Eteocretans, 'true Cretans', were descendants of Crete's pre-Greek population who lived in the east of the island in historical times. Their centre was Praisos, and they wrote inscriptions in the Greek alphabet in a still-undeciphered language, Eteocretan, down to the 3rd…

eisack.s: The Eisack, in Italian Isarco, is a river in South Tyrol, northern Italy, flowing about 96 kilometres from the Brenner Pass to join the Adige near Bolzano. Its valley carries the main road and railway over the Brenner, the chief route between Germany and Italy since Roman…

eichstatt.s: Eichstätt is a town in the Altmühl valley in Upper Bavaria, Germany. Saint Boniface made it a bishopric in the 740s under his kinsman Willibald, and its prince-bishops ruled the surrounding territory until 1802.

erard-de-la-marck.s: Erard de la Marck was prince-bishop of Liège from 1505 to 1538 and a cardinal from 1520. After an early alliance with France he sided with Charles V, while keeping the principality largely neutral between France and the Habsburgs.

eutin.s: Eutin is a town among the lakes of Holstein in Schleswig-Holstein, Germany. From the 14th century it was the residence of the prince-bishops of Lübeck, and later of the Oldenburg Principality of Lübeck.

egge-hills.s: The Egge Hills are a low wooded range of sandstone hills in eastern North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, running south from the Teutoburg Forest. They formed the eastern side of the prince-bishopric of Paderborn, whose capital lies on the plain to the west.

evermod.s: Evermod was a Premonstratensian canon and disciple of Saint Norbert who became the first bishop of Ratzeburg in 1154. Appointed under Henry the Lion, he organised the mission among the Polabian Slavs and began the cathedral.

ellwangen.s: Ellwangen is a town on the Jagst in eastern Baden-Württemberg, Germany. It grew around a Benedictine abbey founded around 764, converted in 1460 into a provostry of noble canons whose prince-provosts ruled the surrounding territory.

elbasan.s: Elbasan is a city in central Albania on the Shkumbin river. As Roman Scampa it was a station on the Via Egnatia, the road across the Balkans from the Adriatic to Constantinople.

elisabeth-christine-of-brunswick-wolfenb.s: Elisabeth Christine of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel was Holy Roman Empress as the wife of Charles VI, whom she married in 1708 after converting from Lutheranism to Catholicism. The daughter of Louis Rudolph of Blankenburg, her only son died in infancy, and under the Pragmatic…

erlangen.s: Erlangen is a city in Middle Franconia, Bavaria, north of Nuremberg. From 1686 the Margrave of Brandenburg-Bayreuth built a planned new town there for Huguenot refugees from France.

eschiva-of-bures.s: Eschiva of Bures was Princess of Galilee in the crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem, heiress of the lordship through her family. Her second husband was Count Raymond III of Tripoli.

einbeck.s: Einbeck is a town in southern Lower Saxony, Germany, in the Leine valley. A member of the Hanseatic League, it was famous from the late Middle Ages for its strong beer, exported widely across northern Europe; the name of Bock beer derives from Einbeck.

eldred-pottinger.s: Eldred Pottinger was an officer of the East India Company's Bombay Artillery who, travelling in disguise, was in Herat when Persia besieged it in 1837–1838 and helped organise its defence. During the First Anglo-Afghan War he served as political agent in Kohistan and survived…

esztergom.s: Esztergom is a city in northern Hungary on the right bank of the Danube, facing Štúrovo in Slovakia. It was the seat of the Árpád grand princes and the first royal capital of Hungary, traditionally the birthplace of Stephen I, and from about 1000 the see of the archbishop and…

ernest-i-duke-of-brunswick-luneburg.s: Ernest I, called the Confessor, was Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, ruling the Principality of Lüneburg from Celle from 1520. A former student at Wittenberg, he introduced the Lutheran Reformation from 1527, signed the Augsburg Confession in 1530 and joined the Schmalkaldic League.

ekaterine-dadiani.s: Ekaterine Dadiani, born Chavchavadze, was the wife of David Dadiani, Prince of Mingrelia, and ruled as regent for their son Niko after her husband's death in 1853. During the Crimean War she led resistance to the Ottoman invasion of Mingrelia.

enguri.s: The Enguri is a river of western Georgia, about 213 km long, rising in the high Caucasus of Svaneti and flowing south-west to the Black Sea. Its lower course long divided Mingrelia from Abkhazia and today marks the line between Georgian-controlled territory and breakaway…

euphrosyne-of-polotsk.s: Euphrosyne of Polotsk was a princess of the Polotsk dynasty who became a nun and founded the Saviour Monastery at Polotsk, where she copied books and kept a school. She commissioned a jewelled reliquary cross, made by the master Lazar Bogsha in 1161 and lost in the Second…

erdmuthe-dorothea-von-zinzendorf.s: Erdmuthe Dorothea von Zinzendorf, born a countess of Reuss-Ebersdorf, married Count Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf in 1722. While her husband led the renewed Moravian Church at Herrnhut and travelled on its missions, she managed the family estates and finances, which kept the…

eldena-abbey.s: Eldena Abbey was a Cistercian monastery near Greifswald on the Pomeranian coast, founded in 1199 under Prince Jaromar I of Rügen. The monks cleared land, promoted German settlement and founded the salt-trading settlement that grew into Greifswald.

emil-hacha.s: Emil Hácha was a Czech lawyer who became President of Czechoslovakia after the Munich Agreement in 1938. Summoned to Berlin in March 1939, he was pressured into accepting German occupation, and he served as state president of the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia under…

edward-hyde-1st-earl-of-clarendon.s: Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon, was an English statesman and historian who advised Charles II in exile and became Lord Chancellor at the Restoration. He was one of the eight Lords Proprietors of Carolina, and his daughter Anne married the future James II, making him…

elizabeth-new-jersey.s: Elizabeth is a city in north-eastern New Jersey, United States, founded in 1664 as Elizabethtown, the first English settlement in the colony. Named after Elizabeth Carteret, wife of the proprietor Sir George Carteret, it was the first capital of New Jersey and of East Jersey.

edward-gibbon-wakefield.s: Edward Gibbon Wakefield was a British colonial theorist who argued that colonial land should be sold at a sufficient price to fund the emigration of free labourers. Developed while he was in prison for abducting an heiress, his ideas shaped the founding of South Australia in…

eliza-lucas-pinckney.s: Eliza Lucas Pinckney was a South Carolina planter who, while managing her father's plantations as a young woman, developed indigo as a commercial crop in the 1740s. Indigo, grown by enslaved workers, became one of the colony's chief exports and greatly enriched the Lowcountry…

eleazar-ben-simon.s: Eleazar ben Simon was a Jewish priest and leader of the Zealots during the First Jewish–Roman War. He gained prominence after the defeat of Cestius Gallus in 66, and from 68 his faction held the inner court of the Temple in Jerusalem, fighting John of Gischala and Simon bar…

emperor-xizong-of-tang.s: Emperor Xizong of Tang, personal name Li Xuan, reigned from 873 to 888. Raised to the throne as a boy, he left government to the eunuch Tian Lingzi while the rebellions of Wang Xianzhi and Huang Chao spread, and when Huang Chao took Chang'an in 881 he fled to Chengdu.

emperor-xizong-of-jin.s: Emperor Xizong of Jin, personal name Wanyan Hela, was the third emperor of the Jurchen Jin dynasty, reigning from 1135 to 1150. A grandson of the founder Aguda, educated in Chinese learning, he centralised government on Tang and Song models, curbing the Jurchen princes, and in…

eidsivating.s: The Eidsivating was the law assembly (thing) of the inland Upplands of eastern Norway in the Middle Ages, meeting at Eidsvoll. Its law, the Eidsivating law, governed Romerike, Hedmark and other inland districts until King Magnus the Lawmender's national law code of 1274…

eidsvoll.s: Eidsvoll is a municipality in Akershus in eastern Norway, on the Vorma river just south of Lake Mjøsa. In the Middle Ages it was the meeting place of the Eidsivating law assembly.

estonians.s: The Estonians are a Finnic people of the eastern Baltic, speaking a language closely related to Finnish, who form the majority of the population of Estonia. Organised in independent parishes and counties until the Northern Crusades, they were conquered by German crusaders and…

errana.s: Errana, or Errapragada, was a 14th-century Telugu poet who completed the Telugu Mahabharata begun by Nannaya and continued by Tikkana. He finished the Aranya Parva, left incomplete by Nannaya, and with the other two is honoured as one of the Kavitrayam, the three poets of the…

enrique-lister.s: Enrique Líster was a Spanish Communist commander in the Spanish Civil War, a former stonemason who rose to lead the 11th Division and later an army corps of the Republic. In August 1937 his troops dissolved the anarchist Regional Defence Council of Aragon, arresting its…

evariste-ndayishimiye.s: Évariste Ndayishimiye is a Burundian politician and former general who became president of Burundi in June 2020. A former fighter of the CNDD-FDD rebel movement during the civil war, he later served as interior minister and secretary-general of the ruling party.

enomoto-takeaki.s: Enomoto Takeaki was a Japanese admiral of the Tokugawa shogunate who refused to surrender its fleet in 1868 and sailed north to Hokkaido. There he was elected president of the Republic of Ezo in 1869 and held out until he surrendered Goryōkaku after the Battle of Hakodate.

ensenada.s: Ensenada is a port city on the Pacific coast of the Mexican state of Baja California, on the Bay of Todos Santos about 100 kilometres south of Tijuana. Named by the Spanish navigator Sebastián Vizcaíno in 1602, it grew after gold was found nearby in the 1870s and was the…

emperor-kanmu.s: Kanmu was emperor of Japan from 781 to 806. To escape the influence of the Buddhist monasteries of Nara, he moved the capital first to Nagaoka-kyō in 784 and then to Heian-kyō, modern Kyoto, in 794, beginning the Heian period.

emperor-shomu.s: Shōmu was emperor of Japan from 724 to 749. A devout Buddhist, he ordered the building of state temples in every province and of Tōdai-ji in Nara, with its colossal bronze statue of the Buddha Vairocana, dedicated in 752.

emil-constantinescu.s: Emil Constantinescu is a Romanian geologist and politician who served as president of Romania from 1996 to 2000. Candidate of the centre-right Romanian Democratic Convention, he defeated Ion Iliescu in 1996, the first peaceful transfer of power to the opposition since the fall…

el-badi-palace.s: The El Badi Palace is a ruined palace in Marrakesh built by the Saadi sultan Ahmad al-Mansur from 1578, after his victory at the Battle of Alcácer Quibir. Decorated with Italian marble, gold and onyx around a vast courtyard of pools and gardens, it was famed as one of the most…

eto-shinpei.s: Etō Shinpei was a samurai of the Saga domain who became a leading statesman of the early Meiji government. As Minister of Justice from 1872 he laid foundations for a modern legal system, but he resigned in 1873 when the government rejected a military expedition to Korea.

eluru.s: Eluru is a city in Andhra Pradesh, India, in the delta region between the Godavari and Krishna rivers. The ancient city of Vengi, capital of the Salankayana dynasty and later of the Eastern Chalukyas, lay close by at the modern village of Pedavegi.

entremont-oppidum.s: Entremont is the site of a fortified hilltop town, or oppidum, on a plateau just north of Aix-en-Provence in southern France. It was the chief stronghold of the Salyes in the 2nd century BCE until Roman armies destroyed it around 123 BCE.

epicurus.s: Epicurus was a Greek philosopher, born on Samos to Athenian settlers, who founded the Epicurean school. After teaching at Mytilene and Lampsacus he settled in Athens around 306 BCE and founded his community, the Garden.

ea-gamil.s: Ea-gamil was the last king of the First Sealand Dynasty, which ruled the marshlands of southern Mesopotamia. According to a Babylonian chronicle he fled to Elam, after which the Kassite Ulamburiash, brother of the Babylonian king Kashtiliash III, conquered the Sealand.

enuma-elish.s: Enuma Elish is the Babylonian epic of creation, named after its opening words 'When on high'. Written in Akkadian on seven tablets, it tells how the god Marduk defeated the primeval sea goddess Tiamat, created the world from her body and was made king of the gods, with Babylon…

ea-mukin-zeri.s: Ea-mukin-zeri was a king of Babylon in the Second Sealand Dynasty who seized the throne after the murder of Simbar-Shipak around 1008 BCE. Babylonian king lists give him a reign of only a few months, and a later chronicle calls him a usurper who was buried in the marshes of…

eildon-hill-north.s: Eildon Hill North is the northernmost of the three Eildon Hills near Melrose in the Scottish Borders. Its summit holds one of the largest hillforts in Scotland, with the platforms of several hundred round-houses, occupied in the Late Bronze Age and the Iron Age.

eildon-hills.s: The Eildon Hills are a group of three volcanic summits above Melrose in the Scottish Borders. Their triple peak gave its name to Trimontium, the Roman fort built beneath them at Newstead.

everglades.s: The Everglades are a vast subtropical wetland in southern Florida, formed by a slow-moving sheet of water flowing from Lake Okeechobee to Florida Bay. In the 19th century they became a refuge for Seminole bands who escaped removal to the west.

esino.s: The Esino is a river of the Marche in central Italy, about 90 km long, flowing into the Adriatic near Falconara. In antiquity, as the Aesis, it marked the southern limit of the land settled by the Senones and later a boundary of Roman Italy.

east-sumatra-revolution.s: The East Sumatra revolution was an uprising in March 1946 in which armed youth groups and leftist militias attacked the Malay and Simalungun aristocracies of eastern Sumatra. Hundreds of members of royal families were killed, among them the poet Amir Hamzah of Langkat.

estahban.s: Estahban is a town in eastern Fars province, Iran, known for its rain-fed fig orchards. Near it stood the fortress of Ij, the capital of the medieval Shabankara rulers of eastern Fars.

enlil.s: Enlil was the chief god of the Sumerian pantheon, lord of the wind and air, whose temple, the Ekur, stood at Nippur. Kings of Sumer and Babylonia sought his recognition at Nippur to legitimise their rule over the land, and in myth he decreed fates and sent the flood.

eshmun.s: Eshmun was the Phoenician god of healing and the chief god of Sidon. His great sanctuary in the Awali valley outside the city was built from the 6th century BCE by kings including Eshmunazar II and Bodashtart and remained a pilgrimage site into Roman times.

easter-island.s: Easter Island, or Rapa Nui, is a remote Polynesian island in the south-eastern Pacific, about 3,500 km west of mainland Chile. Settled by Polynesians around 1200 CE, it is famous for the moai, nearly a thousand giant stone statues of ancestors.

eugenio-matte.s: Eugenio Matte Hurtado (1895–1934) was a Chilean lawyer and socialist politician, grand master of the Grand Lodge of Chile. He took part in the coup of 4 June 1932 that created the Socialist Republic of Chile and sat on its governing junta until Carlos Dávila ousted him and…

elena-ceausescu.s: Elena Ceaușescu (1916–1989) was the wife of the Romanian communist leader Nicolae Ceaușescu and from the 1970s the second most powerful person in the country, as a member of the party's top body and first deputy prime minister. Despite little formal schooling she was promoted…

emperor-chokei.s: Emperor Chōkei (1343–1394) was the third emperor of the Southern Court of Japan, reigning from 1368 to 1383 after his father Go-Murakami. A firm opponent of compromise with the Ashikaga shogunate, he was officially recognised as a legitimate emperor only in 1926, after…

emperor-go-kameyama.s: Emperor Go-Kameyama (died 1424) was the fourth and last emperor of the Southern Court of Japan, reigning from 1383 to 1392. Militarily weakened, he accepted the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu's offer to reunite the two courts, handing the imperial regalia to the Northern emperor…

emperor-go-murakami.s: Emperor Go-Murakami (1328–1368) was the second emperor of the Southern Court of Japan, reigning from 1339 to 1368 after his father Go-Daigo. Based mostly in the mountains of Yoshino and later Anō, he relied on loyalist warrior families such as the Kitabatake and Kusunoki, and…

eight-friends-of-jingling.s: The Eight Friends of Jingling were a group of writers who gathered in the 480s at the residence of Xiao Ziliang, Prince of Jingling, under the Southern Qi dynasty. They were Xiao Yan, Shen Yue, Xie Tiao, Wang Rong, Xiao Chen, Fan Yun, Ren Fang and Lu Chui.

elbe.s: The Elbe is a major river of central Europe, about 1,100 km long, rising in the Giant Mountains of the Czech Republic and flowing through Germany to the North Sea below Hamburg. In Roman times it marked the limit of Augustus's attempted conquest of Germania, and in the early…

eswatini.s: Eswatini, known until 2018 as Swaziland, is a landlocked kingdom in southern Africa between South Africa and Mozambique. Formed by the Dlamini kings in the 18th and 19th centuries, it was a British protectorate from 1903 and became independent in 1968.

ernst-gluck.s: Ernst Glück was a German Lutheran pastor in Swedish Livonia who translated the Bible into Latvian, published in 1685–1694, and worked on an Estonian translation. Based at Marienburg (Alūksne), he also founded schools for Latvian peasants.

epipolae.s: Epipolae is the limestone plateau that rises above the ancient city of Syracuse in Sicily. During the Athenian siege of 415–413 BCE control of the heights decided the struggle.

emilio-jacinto.s: Emilio Jacinto was a Filipino revolutionary and the leading intellectual of the Katipunan, the secret society that launched the revolution against Spain in 1896. A close aide of Andrés Bonifacio, he wrote the Kartilya ng Katipunan, the society's code of conduct, and edited its…

ermengol-vi-of-urgell.s: Ermengol VI of Urgell (1096–1154), called 'of Castile', was Count of Urgell in Catalonia from 1102. Raised partly in Castile, he served the Castilian kings and held lands there, including Valladolid, while extending Urgell southwards against the Muslims.

el-carambolo-treasure.s: The El Carambolo treasure is a hoard of 21 gold objects found in 1958 on the El Carambolo hill at Camas, near Seville, Spain. Dated broadly to the 7th and 6th centuries BCE and including pectorals, bracelets and a necklace with seal-shaped pendants, it is the best-known…

ekoji-i.s: Ekoji I, also called Venkoji, was the founder of the Maratha Bhonsle dynasty of Thanjavur in southern India. A half-brother of Shivaji and son of Shahaji, he served the Bijapur Sultanate as a general and in 1674–1675 seized Thanjavur from its Nayak rulers.

euphemius.s: Euphemius was a Byzantine naval commander in Sicily who rebelled against the emperor Michael II in 826 and proclaimed himself emperor. Defeated by loyal forces, he invited the Aghlabids of Ifriqiya to intervene, and their invasion in 827 began the Muslim conquest of Sicily.

eros.s: Eros was the Greek god of love and desire, in early myth a primeval force and later the son of Aphrodite, shown as a winged youth with bow and arrows. The Boeotian city of Thespiae was his chief cult centre, with a famous statue by Praxiteles and a festival, the Erotidia.

edfu.s: Edfu is a town on the west bank of the Nile in Upper Egypt, between Luxor and Aswan. It is known for its Temple of Horus, built under the Ptolemies between 237 and 57 BCE and the best preserved temple of ancient Egypt, whose sanctuary holds a granite shrine of Nectanebo II.

evgeni-gegechkori.s: Evgeni Gegechkori was a Georgian Menshevik politician who chaired the Transcaucasian Commissariat, the regional government set up in Tiflis in November 1917 after the Bolshevik seizure of power in Petrograd. He later served as foreign minister of the Democratic Republic of…

epi-olmec-culture.s: The Epi-Olmec culture followed the Olmec civilisation in the Gulf Coast lowlands of southern Veracruz and Tabasco in Mexico, from about 300 BCE to 250 CE, with centres such as Tres Zapotes and Cerro de las Mesas. It is known for an early writing system, the Isthmian or…

enewetak.s: Enewetak is a large coral atoll in the Marshall Islands. American forces captured it from Japan in February 1944, and from 1948 to 1958 the United States carried out 43 nuclear tests there, including Ivy Mike in 1952, the first full-scale hydrogen bomb.

equatoria.s: Equatoria is a region in the far south of present-day South Sudan. It was organised as a province of the Egyptian Sudan in the 1870s, first under Samuel Baker and then Charles Gordon, to extend Egyptian rule up the White Nile and suppress the slave trade.

erdene-zuu.s: Erdene Zuu is the oldest surviving Buddhist monastery in Mongolia, founded around 1585 by Abtai Sain Khan beside the ruins of the Mongol capital Karakorum, partly with stones from the old city. Its square enclosure is marked by a wall with 108 stupas.

evagoras-i.s: Evagoras I was king of Salamis in Cyprus from 411 to 374 BCE. He promoted Greek culture, extended his rule over much of the island and allied with Athens and with Egypt against the Achaemenid Empire.

echigo-province.s: Echigo Province was a province of Japan on the Sea of Japan coast, corresponding to most of modern Niigata Prefecture. In the 16th century it was the power base of Uesugi Kenshin, who ruled from Kasugayama Castle and drew wealth from ramie cloth and mines.

etchu-province.s: Etchū Province was a province of Japan on the Sea of Japan coast, corresponding to modern Toyama Prefecture. In the 1570s Uesugi Kenshin of neighbouring Echigo campaigned there against local lords and the Ikkō-ikki.

enna-cennselach.s: Énna Cennselach was a king of Leinster in early medieval Ireland, said to have lived in the 5th century. Irish annals and genealogies remember him as a warlike ruler and as the ancestor of the Uí Chennselaig, the dynasty that dominated southern Leinster and later produced the…

enmetena.s: Enmetena was a ruler of the Sumerian city-state of Lagash around 2400 BCE and a nephew of Eannatum. His inscriptions, especially a clay cone now in the Louvre, record Lagash's long border war with Umma over the fertile Gu-edena plain and the settlement that ended it, often…

easter-rising.s: The Easter Rising was an armed insurrection in Dublin in April 1916, launched by Irish republicans of the Irish Volunteers and the Irish Citizen Army to end British rule. Patrick Pearse proclaimed an Irish Republic from the General Post Office, but the rebels surrendered after…

eanna.s: The Eanna, 'House of Heaven', was the great temple precinct of the goddess Inanna in the Sumerian city of Uruk. Its monumental buildings of the 4th millennium BCE, decorated with cone mosaics, are among the earliest in Mesopotamia, and they yielded the oldest proto-cuneiform…

enmerkar.s: Enmerkar was a legendary king of Uruk, listed in the Sumerian King List and remembered in Sumerian epic poems as a son of the sun god Utu. The poem Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta describes his contest with the distant land of Aratta for precious stones and credits him with…

ehime-prefecture.s: Ehime Prefecture is a prefecture of Japan in the north-west of the island of Shikoku, with its capital at Matsuyama. It covers the old province of Iyo and was formed in 1873 from prefectures created after the abolition of the domains in 1871, including those of Matsuyama,…

el-greco.s: El Greco, born Domenikos Theotokopoulos at Candia in Venetian Crete, was a painter who trained in the Cretan school of icon painting before working in Venice and Rome. From 1577 he settled in Toledo in Spain, where he produced his greatest works, including The Burial of the…

enrico-pescatore.s: Enrico Pescatore was a Genoese adventurer and corsair who held the title Count of Malta. After the Fourth Crusade, with Genoese backing, he occupied much of Crete around 1206 in defiance of Venice, which had bought the claim to the island.

erotokritos.s: Erotokritos is a verse romance in the Cretan dialect of Greek written by Vitsentzos Kornaros in the early 17th century under Venetian rule. Its more than 10,000 rhyming fifteen-syllable lines tell of the love of Erotokritos for the princess Aretousa and his trials to win her.

ethan-allen.s: Ethan Allen was an American frontiersman, land speculator and revolutionary leader, a founder of Vermont. As leader of the Green Mountain Boys he resisted New York's claims to the New Hampshire Grants and in 1775 captured Fort Ticonderoga.

ermengarde-of-narbonne.s: Ermengarde was viscountess of Narbonne from 1134 to 1192 and one of the most powerful women of 12th-century southern France. east-lothian.s: East Lothian is a council area of south-eastern Scotland, east of Edinburgh on the southern shore of the Firth of Forth, with Haddington as its historic county town. It contains the Iron Age hillfort of Traprain Law, a centre of the Votadini, and the site of the Battle of…

edinburgh.s: Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland, on the southern shore of the Firth of Forth. Its castle rock was Din Eidyn, the stronghold of the British kingdom of Gododdin, until the Northumbrians took it, probably in 638.

el-castillo-de-huarmey.s: El Castillo de Huarmey is an archaeological site on the north coast of Peru, in the Áncash region, belonging to the Wari Empire. In 2012 archaeologists found an unlooted royal tomb there holding the remains of 58 elite women, some regarded as queens, buried with gold and…

ebrohimi.s: Ebrohimi was the fortified town of the Itsekiri merchant and governor of the river Nana Olomu, on a creek of the Benin River in the western Niger Delta. From there Nana controlled the palm-oil trade between the interior and European firms.

empress-dowager-bo.s: Empress Dowager Bo, born Bo Ji, was a consort of Liu Bang, founder of the Han dynasty, and the mother of Emperor Wen. Originally a concubine of Wei Bao, king of Western Wei, she entered Liu Bang's palace after Wei Bao's defeat and bore him a son, Liu Heng.

edict-of-pitres.s: The Edict of Pîtres was a set of laws issued by the West Frankish king Charles the Bald at an assembly at Pîtres on the Seine in June 864. It reformed the coinage, ordering a standard silver penny struck at a limited number of mints, and ordered fortified bridges on the rivers…

emperor-ruizong-of-tang.s: Emperor Ruizong of Tang (662–716), born Li Dan, was a son of Emperor Gaozong and Wu Zetian. Placed on the throne by his mother in 684, he reigned only as a figurehead and yielded the throne to her when she founded her own Zhou dynasty in 690.

emperor-zhongzong-of-tang.s: Emperor Zhongzong of Tang (656–710) was a son of Emperor Gaozong and Wu Zetian. He succeeded his father at the end of 683 but was deposed by his mother early in 684 and sent into exile.

erlitou-culture.s: The Erlitou culture was an early Bronze Age society of the Yellow River valley, named after its type site near Yanshi in the Luoyang basin of Henan, and dated roughly 1900–1500 BCE. Its centre had palace compounds on rammed-earth platforms, foundries producing the earliest…

emperor-tenmu.s: Emperor Tenmu (c. 631–686) was the 40th emperor of Japan, reigning from 673 to 686.

emperor-yuryaku.s: Emperor Yūryaku was the 21st emperor of Japan in traditional reckoning, who probably reigned in the later 5th century. He is generally identified with King Bu of Wa in Chinese records and with the great king Wakatakeru named on the Inariyama and Eta Funayama swords, evidence…

emperor-xuanzong-of-jin.s: Emperor Xuanzong of Jin (1163–1224), personal name Wanyan Xun, was emperor of the Jurchen Jin dynasty from 1213 to 1224. Placed on the throne after a coup killed his predecessor during the Mongol invasion, he bought a truce from Genghis Khan in 1214 with tribute and a…

ezra.s: Ezra was a Jewish priest and scribe who, according to the Hebrew Bible, came from Babylonia to Jerusalem in the Persian period with authority from the Achaemenid king Artaxerxes. He is credited with reading the law of Moses to the people and enforcing it, including the…

e-e-evans-pritchard.s: Sir Edward Evan Evans-Pritchard (1902–1973) was a British social anthropologist and professor at Oxford. His studies of the peoples of southern Sudan, especially Witchcraft, Oracles and Magic among the Azande (1937) and The Nuer (1940), became classics of anthropology.

eshowe.s: Eshowe is a town in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, in the hills north of the Thukela river. During the Anglo-Zulu War a British column was besieged at its mission station for more than two months in 1879, and from 1887 it was the seat of the British administration of Zululand.

ecuadorian-peruvian-war.s: The Ecuadorian–Peruvian War was a border war fought in July 1941 between Ecuador and Peru over disputed Amazonian and coastal territory. eritrean-war-of-independence.s: The Eritrean War of Independence was a thirty-year struggle by Eritrean nationalist fronts against Ethiopia, which had annexed Eritrea in 1962. ecuadorian-war-of-independence.s: The Ecuadorian War of Independence was fought between 1820 and 1822 to free the Royal Audience of Quito from Spanish rule. ethiopian-mahdist-war.s: The Ethiopian–Mahdist War was fought between the Ethiopian Empire and the Mahdist State of Sudan. After the Ethiopians helped evacuate Egyptian garrisons, Mahdist forces raided Ethiopia and sacked Gondar in 1888.
